about: What the app can do “My Budget” isn't a spending log — it's a full budget built on the envelope method. It can do a lot, and most of it isn't buried deep in menus but hidden in gestures and small touches. This page is a quick tour; after that, each screen gets its own article. The essentials Expense tracking answers the question “where did the money go”. A budget answers a more important one: **“what can it still cover”** — today, until payday, before your vacation.   Envelopes Every dollar gets a job: groceries, rent, vacation. You see how much is left in each envelope, and overspending turns red right away. More in [“How the budget works”](start.md).  Your data is yours Your budget lives on your phone and in your cloud. The developer has no access to it. You can lock the cloud with a password — AES-256. More in [“Cloud and backups”](sync.md#password).  Moving from YNAB Accounts, categories and your whole history from YNAB 4 or web YNAB move over as a file, and a small glossary shows what familiar terms are called here. More in [“First steps”](first-steps.md). Quick entry It's easier to record a purchase at the checkout than to remember it in the evening. That's why there are several ways to do it.   To the inbox No time to pick a category and account at the checkout? Just enter the amount. The “To inbox” button saves it marked “Sort”, and at home the form opens these transactions one by one. Turn it on in “Settings → Data → Inbox”. More in [“Transaction form”](entry.md#inbox).  By voice “Whole Foods 70 groceries from account Checking” — and the form is filled in. More in [“Voice input”](voice.md).  From a receipt Point the camera at the receipt's QR code — the amount and date fill in by themselves, and from the second time on the app recognizes the store by its register. Works where the app can read your country's receipts. More in [“Receipt scanner”](receipt.md).  From the home screen Widgets and shortcuts open the form with one tap, without going into the app. More in [“Widgets and shortcuts”](widgets.md).  Calculator keypad Amounts are typed on the app's own keypad with addition and subtraction, split across several categories, transferred between accounts — even in different currencies. More in [“Transaction form”](entry.md). Plans   Goals Five kinds: monthly, by a date, keep a balance, percent of income, and a shopping list. The app works out how much to set aside. More in [“Goals”](goals.md).  Scheduled payments Rent, subscriptions, loan payments — with a reminder ahead of time and entered in one tap. More in [“Scheduled payments”](scheduled.md).  Credit cards and debt Money for paying off a credit card is set aside automatically, and you see the debt month by month. More in the scenario [“Credit cards and debt”](scenario-credit.md).  Tags and “who owes whom” A trip, a renovation, shared costs with friends — a tag gathers them from different categories and works out who owes whom. More in [“Payees and tags”](payees-tags.md). Reports Ten reports: where the money went, trend and deviation from usual, money flow from income to spending, income and expenses by month, age of money, net worth, credit card debt. And “Overview” is your home screen: you pick the blocks and arrange them yourself. More in [“Reports”](reports.md) and [“Overview”](overview.md). Devices and cloud One budget on your phone, tablet and Windows computer — for two or for the whole family. Sync through Google Drive, Dropbox or WebDAV — Nextcloud, ownCloud, pCloud, your own server; backups are made automatically on a schedule. More in the scenarios [“One budget on several devices”](scenario-devices.md) and [“Two or more people, one budget”](scenario-together.md). Make it yours Thirteen languages, sixty currencies, amount and date formats for your country. Seven styles in light and dark, fonts, density, corner shapes, icons. Several budgets: personal, family, work. More in [“Settings”](settings.md). Where to start  [“How the budget works”](start.md) — the envelope method in ten minutes. [“First steps”](first-steps.md) — from installing to your first month. [Scenarios](scenario-paycheck.md) — ready-made answers: paycheck to paycheck, freelancing, credit cards, a trip with friends.
start: How the budget works The envelope method in ten minutes: where money comes in, how to divide it up, and what happens when the month turns over. Envelopes: the big idea Imagine you took your paycheck out in cash and split it into envelopes: “Groceries”, “Utilities”, “Vacation”. When you buy groceries, you take money only from that envelope. An empty envelope means there's no more money for that. The app does exactly this, just without the paper.   Money in your accounts Checking — $1,700 Cash — $200  “Unassigned” $1,900 — no job yet  Category envelopes Groceries — $550 Utilities — $170 …and so on, until it reaches 0  Spending You bought bread — the “Groceries” envelope got thinner Every dollar in your accounts sits in exactly one place: either in some envelope or in “unassigned”. So at any moment you can see what you can still afford and what you can't. The first goal is to bring “unassigned” down to zero: then **every dollar has a job**. That's not the finish line but the first step — where the method takes you next is [at the end of the article](#ladder). How this differs from the usual “expense tracking” is [below](#vs). How this differs from expense tracking Many people log their spending for years — in a notebook, a spreadsheet, their bank's app — and still can't see why the money runs out before the month does. Expense tracking honestly tells you about the past. Envelopes help you steer the future.    Example: “there's still plenty in checking” It's the middle of the month and there's $1,400 in checking. You want headphones for $280.  **Expense tracking** sees $1,400 and says: “go ahead”. But rent is due in a week — $800, plus utilities and groceries until payday. The headphones are bought, and rent is short. **Envelopes** see the same $1,400, but divided up: “Rent” — $800, “Utilities” — $170, “Groceries” — $260, “Fun & hobbies” — $170. There's $170 free for headphones. Want to buy them now? Decide which envelope the missing $110 comes from. You make the decision, and you make it before buying, not after.  So is there expense tracking here? Yes — and in more detail than a notebook.  Every purchase is recorded, and “Where the money went”, “Month spending” and the reports show where it all went. It's just not the goal here but a check of the plan: did what you decided match what happened? Next month you'll budget more precisely.  In short Expense tracking is the rearview mirror. Envelopes are the steering wheel.  Looking in the mirror is useful: you see where you came from. But only the wheel helps you move forward — a decision about where the money goes, made in advance. Three numbers for every category Turn your phone sideways — the “Budget” screen becomes a table, and the envelope's three numbers are labeled right in the column headers.   **“Planned”** — how much you put into the envelope this month. It's a decision: “$100 for utilities in November”. **“Spent”** — how much has already left the envelope: all spending in this category this month, with a minus sign. A refund for a returned item reduces this number. **“Available”** — how much you can still spend: carried over from last month + planned − spent.  In the screenshot, “Utilities” shows planned 100, spent 92.74 — so you'd think 7.26 is left. But 29.44 is available: $22.18 went unspent in October and carried over into November. That's how an envelope builds up. A green chip means there's money in the envelope, a gray zero means it's empty, and red means a minus: you spent more than there was.   What it looks like on screen and what to tap is in the article [“Budget”](budget.md). Here are just the rules the numbers follow.  Income goes to “unassigned”, not to a category Your paycheck doesn't land in an envelope by itself: it goes to “unassigned”, and you divide it up.  In the transaction form, income is recorded to “Income for November” by default — that is, to this month's “unassigned”. You can also choose “Income for December” — see the section [“Age of money in detail”](overview.md) of the “Overview” article.  A refund goes back to the envelope Got money back for a returned item? It goes to the category it left from, not to income.  How to record it — the article [“Transaction form”](entry.md), section “Refund for a returned item”.  A transfer isn't spending You withdrew cash, paid off a credit card, moved money to savings — the money is still yours.  A transfer between budget accounts doesn't touch any envelope. Only a transfer to an account outside the budget (savings, a deposit) leaves the envelopes — then the app asks for a category. Month after month The budget lives in months. What happens to an envelope when the month turns over is one of the key rules.  A plus carries over Didn't spend it all? The rest moves into the next month and stays in the envelope.  That's how you save for big and irregular things: put $150 into “Vacation” every month, don't spend it — and by summer there's $900. You can also set money aside for the future right away: you can assign money to any month ahead — the “›” arrow on the “Budget” screen.  A minus resets to zero Spent more than the envelope had? The category turns red. When the month turns over, the minus is wiped — but not without a trace.  A minus from your own money (red, wallet icon) reduces next month's “unassigned”: the money is already spent, after all. So it's better to cover a minus right away by moving money from another category: tap the red amount on the “Budget” screen. A minus on a credit card (yellow, card icon) is a different story: it doesn't eat your money, it grows the card debt. “Unassigned” doesn't take it, but the debt will still have to be paid.  “Month budget” on “Overview” The whole month's bookkeeping as one ladder: carried over from last month, income, assigned, and the “unassigned” total.  If the number on the chip looks odd, look here: you'll see where it came from. More in the article [“Overview”](overview.md). A credit card in the budget The credit card is the least familiar part of the envelope method. There's one rule: a purchase on a credit card spends envelope money just like a purchase on a debit card.  The purchase You bought groceries on a credit card for $35 — the “Groceries” envelope got $35 thinner, as usual.  Money for the payment sets itself aside The app moves these $35 into the “Card payments” group, into your credit card's category.  So by the payment date the money for paying it off is already set apart, and you can't spend it by accident. You don't need to put anything aside yourself.  Paying the card Pay off the credit card with a transfer from your regular account to the credit card. The money set aside goes to the payment.  How to record a transfer — the article [“Transaction form”](entry.md). The method's four rules The app doesn't force you to follow them — it suggests them one at a time, when a rule becomes relevant.   Give every dollar a job Keep assigning money until “unassigned” is zero. Money without a job slips away unnoticed.  Embrace your true expenses Insurance once a year, a car repair, holiday gifts — these are expenses too. Set aside a little for them every month.  “By date” goals help: the app works out how much to put in each month to make it in time.  Roll with the punches Overspending isn't failure. Move money from another envelope and carry on.  A budget is a plan, not a vow. What matters is that the envelopes honestly show how much is left.  Age your money The goal is to spend money you earned a month ago, not yesterday.  “Age of money” on “Overview” keeps track of this. Once it reaches 30 days, you can live on last month's money: details in the article [“Overview”](overview.md). Zero is only the first step “Unassigned” at zero is a good goal, but not the final one. The method goes further: from “I make it to payday” to “my money works for me”. The steps come in order — skipping them is risky: investing without a cushion means selling your investments the first time the car breaks down.  Every dollar has a job All the money in your accounts is split into envelopes. You know what you can afford until the end of the month. **How to tell you're here:** “unassigned” is zero, and no categories are red. **How the app helps:** the “Unassigned” chip, auto-assign, “Cover all overspending”.  Envelopes for irregular expenses Insurance, car repairs, gifts and vacations no longer catch you off guard: a little goes toward them every month. **How to tell you're here:** a big bill arrives, and the money for it is already waiting in its envelope. **How the app helps:** the goals “By date” and “Monthly” work out how much to put in; the “What’s ahead” block on “Overview” reminds you where money is short.  A month ahead You spend money you earned a month ago. This month doesn't need the new paycheck — it goes to the next one. **How to tell you're here:** “Age of money” is 30 days or more. **How the app helps:** “Age of money” on “Overview”, income “for next month” in the form — details in the article [“Overview”](overview.md), section “Age of money in detail”.  An emergency fund A reserve of three to six months of normal spending. Losing a job or getting sick becomes a setback, not a disaster. **How to tell you're here:** “Rainy day fund” holds several months' worth of expenses. **How the app helps:** a “Balance” goal on the “Rainy day fund” category; average monthly spending — in the reports and on the category screen.  Your money works for you The cushion is built, irregular expenses are covered, you're a month ahead — and now the extra can do more than sit: a deposit, bonds, investments. Money starts making money. **How to tell you're here:** every month part of your income goes to “Investments”, and you don't touch it for everyday spending. **How the app helps:** the “Savings” group with an “Investments” category; “Pay yourself” on “Overview” shows what percent of your income you set aside (the norm is 10% or more); a “Tracking” account for a deposit or brokerage account; “Net worth” on “Overview” — how everything you own grows. How long the road takes depends on your income and habits. The first step is usually the first month. A month ahead takes anywhere from three months to a year. What matters is taking a step every month, not a leap. Ready to start? Next — [“First steps”](first-steps.md): from the first launch to your first month.
first-steps: First steps From the first launch to a working budget: the setup wizard, the “First steps” list, and what to do in your first month. First launch: how would you like to start On first launch the setup wizard opens. The first screen offers three doors. You can change the language right here with the button in the top right corner: the categories the app suggests by default will be in that language too.    “Starting from scratch” The wizard walks you through five steps: currency and name, accounts, categories, your first assignment. The steps are explained below.  “I already have a budget” You've kept a budget on another phone or before reinstalling. The app loads it from the cloud — Google Drive, Dropbox or WebDAV — or from a backup file.  The name isn't asked here: it comes with the budget and serves as the address of its folder in the cloud.  “I’m moving from YNAB” YNAB 4 or web YNAB: accounts, categories and history come over from a file.  First the currency and name, then you pick the export file, and at the end there's a glossary: what each YNAB term is called here. You can open the glossary later too, when importing from settings. About five minutes. You can skip any step — the “First steps” list on “Overview” will remind you what's left. Starting from scratch: five steps At the bottom of each step are “Next” and “Skip”. The system Back button takes you one step back instead of closing the app.    Step 2. Currency and name The app fills in the currency from your phone's country — check it. This is the symbol you keep your budget in; the app doesn't convert amounts.  Come up with a name of your own: “Family”, “Personal”. Leave the field empty and the budget will be called “Main budget”. The name shows in the header and in the cloud folder name, so it's easy to recognize the budget on any device.    Step 3. Where your money is Add every place you keep money, with today's balance: your wallet, cards at every bank, a credit card, savings.  Leave out even one card, and the budget won't match what you actually have. Tap “+” next to a matching template — the new account sheet opens with the type already chosen. The account balance goes straight into “unassigned” — in the screenshot, two accounts brought in $1,900. More about accounts in the article [“Accounts”](accounts.md).    Step 4. Your categories The “What you spend on” chips add the categories you need: “Car”, “Kids”, “Pets”. Below is the whole list, and you can adjust it to suit you.   tap a category to rename it; the cross removes a category; “Add a category” is in every group, “Add a new group” is at the bottom; the pencil next to a group name — rename the group. The screenshot shows the start of the list; it's longer.    Step 5. Assign your money Divide “unassigned” among the envelopes: tap the amount next to a category and enter how much you're ready to spend on it this month.  The top shows how much is left. In the screenshot, $840 is assigned and $1,060 is left. You don't have to reach zero here: start with the essentials — housing, food, phone — and assign the rest later on the “Budget” screen.    Step 6. All set The main rule once more: keep assigning money until “unassigned” reaches zero.  “Open budget” takes you to the “Budget” screen. From there the app gives hints as you go — one hint at a time, when it's relevant. After the wizard: the “First steps” list A list card appears at the top of “Overview”. It holds what the budget needs before it can show the truth. The wizard counts what you've already done in it.    **Cash in your wallet** — Your wallet as a separate account. Cash is the first thing to go missing: without its own account, the budget drifts away from the money in your hands with the very first purchase. No cash? — “No cash”. **Cards from every bank** — All cards and accounts are added. If you added them in the wizard, the item is already checked. **Categories that fit you** — The category list is adjusted. Went through the categories step — it's checked. The button opens the same screen as in the wizard. A category that already has transactions isn't deleted by the cross but hidden: the transactions stay where they are. **Money assigned** — “Unassigned” has reached zero. Until then, the item shows how much is left and takes you to “Budget”. **First transaction** — You've recorded your first purchase — the budget has come to life. The button opens the form. **A copy off the phone** — A cloud or a backup file. Lose your phone — and the budget isn't lost. Buttons: connect a cloud or “Backups”.  Done items get a check mark At the top, “3 of 6”: how many are done. A finished item is a single line with a check mark.  One item is expanded The first unfinished one — or the one you tapped. It says what to do and why.  The main button is a door It leads straight to where the item gets done: the account form, “Budget”, the transaction form, cloud sign-in. Sometimes there's a second one next to it — your answer: “No cash”, “All added”, “Keep as is”.  Hide the list Card menu → “Hide the list” (with “Undo” at the bottom of the screen). Once everything is done, the card says “Your budget is set up” — tap “Got it”.  While the list is open, the regular hints on “Overview” stay quiet — so the same thing isn't said twice. To bring all hints back: “Settings → Help & contact → Hints → Show hints again”. If you moved from YNAB, the list is different: reconciling account balances with the bank, cash, assigning and a backup — the accounts and categories already came over in the file. Your first month  **Record every purchase** — right away, at the checkout: “+ Transaction”, the camera for a receipt, or the microphone. Five seconds now instead of an evening with a bank statement later. No time? — “Inbox” (article [“Transaction form”](entry.md)). **Money came in — divide it up.** Every paycheck lands in “unassigned”; hand it out to the envelopes on the “Budget” screen. **An envelope turned red — move money** from another one. That's normal: the first month always shows what you underestimated. **Once a week, reconcile your accounts** with the bank — account menu, “Balance reconciliation” (article [“Accounts”](accounts.md)). **At the end of the month, look at “Overview”**: “Where the money went”, “Month spending”. Next month you'll assign based on experience.
scenario-devices: One budget on several devices A phone in your pocket, a tablet at home, a computer at work — and the same budget on all of them. Record a purchase at the checkout, and by evening it's on your laptop. How to set it up and what to keep in mind. Who needs this   Phone and computer Spending from the phone, at the checkout. Planning the month, reports and reviews on a big screen. For the computer there's the “Windows version”: the same budget, its own look made for a mouse. It syncs through Google Drive — if a computer is involved, choose that cloud on the phone too.  Phone and tablet Dividing a paycheck among envelopes is comfortable on a tablet: “Budget” in landscape is a full-screen table.  A new phone The old one broke or you upgraded — years of budget move over in a couple of minutes. It's the same scenario: the new phone is the second device. A cloud connects the devices: Google Drive, Dropbox or WebDAV (Nextcloud, ownCloud, pCloud, your own server). Each device sends its edits there and picks up the others'. How it works in detail — in the article [“Cloud and backups”](sync.md). On the first device The one where you already keep the budget.   “Settings”, “Sync” section → “Authorization”. Sign in to the cloud. For Google Drive — with the Google account you'll use on the other devices too. For Dropbox — with your Dropbox username and password, not through Google. Will there be a Windows computer? Choose Google Drive: the Windows version doesn't connect to other clouds. Want to lock the data in the cloud with a password? — “Set a password” in the “Cloud encryption” block. Write the password down: nobody can recover it. Go back to “Overview” and tap the sync icon in the top right. The budget goes to the cloud.  On the second device  The app was just installed  In the first-launch wizard, choose “I already have a budget”. “Load budget from cloud” opens. Connect **the same** cloud with **the same** account. Pick the budget in the list and tap “Load budget”. If a password is set on the first device, set the same one here. Check the currency: “Settings” → “Budget currency”. Details — [below](#per-device).   The app is already installed, with its own budget “Settings”, “Sync” section → “Load budget from cloud” — then the same steps. Or tap the budget name in the “Overview” header — “Load budget from cloud” is there too.  If a budget with the same name on this device already has its own data, on the first sync the app asks whether it's one budget or two different ones: “From cloud” or “Merge”. More in the article [“Cloud and backups”](sync.md#trouble). What's shared and what each device keeps to itself What syncs is the **budget data**. Appearance and security settings don't: each device has its own.    Budget currency — check it on every device The budget currency symbol lives on the device and doesn't go to the cloud. A loaded budget gets the currency of the budget that was already on this device — usually based on the phone's country. The amounts don't change, only the symbol next to them. Wrong symbol? — “Settings” → “Budget currency”.  Receipt photos Right after installing, photos stay on the device where they were taken. For them to appear everywhere, turn on “Sync photos” on the “Sync” screen — on **every** device. Every day  You'll rarely need to sync by hand The app syncs by itself — a few seconds after every time you open it. The number on the sync icon on “Overview” is how many of your edits haven't gone to the cloud yet.  Recorded a purchase and putting the phone away Once the app is minimized, Android doesn't let it keep working, so the edits go up the next time you open it. If you're about to sit down at your computer, tap the sync icon on the phone so the purchase is already there.  The sync icon's color Flashed green — all good. Red — it didn't work; a single failure usually just means no network. If the icon stays red, sync has failed several times in a row — open the “Sync” screen, it says what happened. Common mistakes   Without a cloud Don't want a cloud? You can move the budget between your own devices directly: as a file or over Wi-Fi on the same network. It's a one-time transfer, not ongoing sync: you'll have to transfer edits again. Good for moving to a new phone. More in the article [“Cloud and backups”](sync.md#local).
scenario-together: Two or more people, one budget A family with shared money: both pay, both record, both see how much is left in each envelope. How to agree with the app and with each other so there's no confusion and no duplicates. Who it's for The money is shared: paychecks are pooled, and rent, food and vacations come from the common pot. Each person pays with their own card or cash, but the envelopes are shared: both see “Groceries”, and whoever hits the limit first is the one who sees red. If each of you also has personal money the other shouldn't see, see the scenario [“Couples: shared costs and personal money”](scenario-couple.md). Setup Technically this is the same budget on several devices — the steps are in the scenario [“One budget on several devices”](scenario-devices.md). There's one difference, and it's important.  A separate cloud account — just for the budget All devices must sign in to the cloud with **one** account. But signing in to the husband's personal Google account on the wife's phone is a bad idea: the phone will start syncing his contacts, photos and email. Create a **new** Google account — just for the budget — and use it to sign in to the app's cloud on every device. Everyone keeps their own personal accounts. Same for Dropbox: a separate Dropbox, signed in with a username and password.  One cloud password for everyone If you set a password, set the **same** one on every phone. The password doesn't sync: it's entered on each device by hand. Who paid for what The app doesn't remember which phone a transaction was recorded on. The **account** is what tells spending apart.  An account for each person Give each person their own accounts: “Olivia's card”, “Peter's card”, “Olivia's cash”. Whichever account a purchase is recorded on, that person paid. Each of you reconciles account balances with your own bank — “Balance reconciliation” in the article [“Accounts”](accounts.md). Whose spending this month — “Activity” → “⋮” → “Filter”, filter by account.  If you need “who owes whom” In a shared budget you usually don't: the money is shared anyway. But if you've agreed to split something in half — a tag with “Settle up” turned on for those purchases shows who owes whom how much. More in the article [“Payees and tags”](payees-tags.md). Assigning money Dividing a paycheck among envelopes is easier for one person — or for two at one screen.  Why not each from your own phone If both of you change how much is set aside in the same category at the same time, whoever's edit reached the cloud last wins — or the app shows a “Conflict” and asks you to choose. The amount in the envelope may not be the one you agreed on. Agree on who does the assigning. Before you start, open the app and give it a couple of seconds to sync — so you see the other person's latest spending.  What both see “Unassigned”, the balance of each envelope, “Overspent” and “Running out” on “Overview” are shared. If “Groceries” turns yellow, both see it, and you're discussing the same numbers. Scheduled payments Rent and subscriptions are shared, and the due date arrives on both phones.  One person confirms If two people tap “Confirm” on the same payment before the phones have synced, the transaction is recorded **twice**. Agree on who confirms scheduled payments, or let the app sync before confirming. Delete the extra transaction in “Activity”. Due date reminders arrive on both phones — for whoever has them turned on. Each person sets them up on their own phone: “Settings” → “Reminders”. Every day  Recorded something? Sync The app syncs when you open it, not when you minimize it. Recorded a big purchase and know the other person is about to look at the budget? Tap the sync icon on “Overview”.  The evening reminder counts you both “Remind me to add spending” stays quiet if the budget already has spending today — including spending entered by the other person and brought in by sync. If you want it to remind each of you, each should record their own spending the same day.  “Recent transactions” are shared On “Overview” you see what the other person bought: their purchases appear there after a sync. Common mistakes
scenario-couple: "Couples: shared costs and personal money" Each of you has your own salary and your own spending, while the apartment, food and vacations are split in half. How to handle this in the app today, what it can't do yet, and how to square up once a month. What works today What you'd like is this: a shared budget, “Our home”, that both of you keep, plus a personal one each that the other can't see. Through one shared cloud that **won't work** — why is below. But it will work if you pass the shared budget over Wi-Fi at home.  Why A phone signs in to the cloud with one account, and every budget on that phone syncs to that cloud. The cloud password is also one per phone, not per budget. So a shared budget in a shared cloud and a personal one hidden from your partner can't live on the same phone: the personal one would go to the same place as the shared one. Three approaches work.   Personal budgets and a “shared” tag Each has their own budget — nobody sees the other's money. Shared spending is marked with a tag, and once a month you compare and even out. Details — [below](#tag).  Two budgets, the shared one over Wi-Fi Each phone has its own budget and the shared “Our home”. Each of you has your own cloud, and you pass the shared budget to each other over Wi-Fi at home. Details — [below](#wifi).  One shared budget for both All the money in one budget, personal money as its own categories. Both see everything. Good if you have nothing to hide from each other. Details — [below](#all-shared). The “shared” tag approach Each has their own budget on their own phone: their own cloud, or no cloud at all. Each records shared spending in their own budget as usual and puts a tag on it.  How to set it up — each on your own phone  Create a category for your share of shared spending — for example, “Family” in the “Fixed expenses” group. Every month, put in as much as you agreed to contribute to the shared pot. Paid for something shared — groceries for home, utilities? Record the purchase in this category. In the “Tags” field, create a “shared” tag and put it on every such purchase. On “Overview”, in the “My tags” block → “⋮” → “Choose tags…”, check “shared”, and set the period to “Total for this month”.  Your personal budget answers the question “how much do I spend”. Your share of the shared home is one line item, like rent: “Family”. If you want to see where the shared money goes, open the “shared” tag screen: it has “By category”. In that case, put shared spending in the regular categories, and the tag will gather it together. End of the month: who owes whom   Each of you checks in “My tags” how much you spent on “shared” this month. Add the two amounts and split in half — that's each person's share. Whoever spent less than their share sends the difference to the other. **Example.** Olivia spent $1,200 on shared costs, Peter spent $800. That's $2,000 in total, so each share is $1,000. Peter sends Olivia $200.  How to record the transfer  **Peter** — a $200 expense in the “Family” category with the “shared” tag: it's also his contribution to the shared pot. **Olivia** — $200 coming in from Peter to the same “Family” category, with the same tag: the money returned to the envelope. How to record a refund to a category — in the article [“Transaction form”](entry.md). In Peter's “My tags” it becomes $1,000. In Olivia's it stays $1,200: the block counts only spending. Her $1,000 is on the “shared” tag screen: “Received” $200 and “Net” $1,000. Compare using “My tags” **before** the transfer — after it, the numbers are already evened out.  “Settle up” calculates “spent minus received” in **your** budget — it's good when you split a cost with someone who doesn't write to your budget: a trip with friends, a group gift. For a couple with two budgets it shows only your half of the picture: the other person's contribution isn't in your budget. So here, compare using “My tags”. About “Settle up” — in the article [“Payees and tags”](payees-tags.md). Two budgets, the shared one over Wi-Fi Each phone has two budgets: your own and the shared “Our home”. Each of you has your own cloud — your own account, your own password. Both budgets go to the phone owner's cloud, and the other person doesn't see them there. You pass only “Our home” to each other — over Wi-Fi, when you're both at home.  How to set it up  Each of you connects a cloud on your own phone with your own account, as usual. Olivia creates the “Our home” budget: tap the budget name in the “Overview” header — there's the list of budgets and a new budget. Peter creates an empty budget with the same name on his phone. The first time, Peter receives “Our home” from Olivia over Wi-Fi (how — below) and chooses “Replace completely”: his empty budget becomes a copy of Olivia's.  Exchanging at home  **Both of you open “Our home”.** The exchange happens between the open budgets. “Settings” → “Local transfer”. Olivia: “Start the server”. Peter: “Scan the QR” → “Receive the data” → “Merge”. Olivia: “Stop the server”. The exchange goes both ways: Peter gets Olivia's edits, and his edits go to Olivia — transactions and receipt photos alike. It doesn't matter which of you sends and which receives.  **“This looks like a different budget” — tap “Cancel”.** If one of you has your own budget open instead of “Our home”, the two budgets share no accounts or transactions, and the app asks before merging. “Continue anyway” would pour personal spending into the shared budget, and there'd be no way to separate it again.  You can't separate them by hand, but you can roll both back to an automatic backup — the app makes these itself, every 5 days by default. The exchange goes both ways, so two budgets are spoiled: Peter's personal one (“Our home” came into it), and Olivia's “Our home” (Peter's personal spending came into it). Each fixes their own on their own phone.  Open the spoiled budget. “Settings” → “Backups”. Find a backup of **this** budget (its name is in the backup's row) dated **before** the exchange. Tap the clock-with-arrow icon → “Restore”. After that, **don't tap “Sync now”**: the merged budget is still in the cloud. Delete this budget's sync file in your cloud — as in the article [“Cloud and backups”](sync.md#rollback), steps 2–4. Each of you has your own cloud, and only your phone writes this budget there, so the part about several devices doesn't apply. Edits made after the backup will be lost. Shared ones can be recovered: once Olivia has rolled back “Our home”, exchange once more with both of you on “Our home”, and the shared edits return to her from Peter's “Our home” — his copy is clean. Personal spending entered after the backup will have to be recorded again. Before the first exchange it's worth making backups by hand — each on your own phone, and of **both** budgets: a backup is made for the open budget. Open your own budget → “Backups” → “Create a backup now”, then open “Our home” and repeat. That way you'd roll back not to a five-day-old automatic backup but to the state right before the exchange.  No. The Wi-Fi transfer is encrypted with the confirmation code from the sending phone's screen; the backup password plays no part in it. The password in the “Cloud encryption” block locks only **your** cloud. It has to be the same only when two phones write to one cloud — here the clouds are different.  Each of you keeps “Our home” on your own phone: record a purchase in the store, and it's immediately in your copy and your cloud. Exchange at home — and both have everything. If one phone still has an older version of the app, the receiver's edits won't go back — the app says so; then exchange again, swapping roles. If you both edited the same transaction, the later edit stays, as with regular sync. The trade-off: the shared budget is in sync only once you're both home and have exchanged. One shared budget for both If there are no personal secrets, it's simplest to keep everything together — then you see the whole picture and a single “unassigned” for both of you.   Setup — as in the scenario [“Two or more people, one budget”](scenario-together.md): a separate cloud account for the budget, signed in on both phones. Personal money — as categories of its own: “Olivia's personal”, “Peter's personal”. Each month the agreed amount goes into them; how to spend it is up to the owner. Accounts — each has their own: “Olivia's card”, “Peter's card”. That way you see who paid. The trade-off: both of you see everything — spending from the “personal” categories and card balances alike. What's not there yet A shared budget that syncs through the cloud for both of you on its own, alongside personal ones hidden from your partner, and moving a shared expense from a personal budget to the shared one in one tap — not there yet. We'll build this when people need it. If that's you, write to “Telegram chat” (“Settings”, “Help & contact” section): the more such messages, the sooner.
scenario-freelance: Freelance and irregular income Money comes in when the client pays: feast one month, famine the next. How to stop living from one payment to the next with an income like that, set money aside for taxes, and know what you really earn. The big idea With a salary, the month is predictable: paid on the 5th, enough until the next 5th. A freelancer doesn't know the month's income in advance — so you can't plan from it. Plan from the money you **already have**.   Spend what you earned earlier The month lives on what came in before. What comes in now works for the next month. [How](#last-month).  Smooth it out with a cushion A good month tops up the reserve, a lean month draws on it. [How](#buffer).  Set the tax aside right away A percentage of each payment goes into its own envelope before the money gets spent. [How](#taxes). Spend last month's money Record each payment not to this month but to the **next** one. Then by the 1st, the whole month is already paid for with money you've earned, and you divide it among the envelopes once — not in pieces after every payment.  How to record a payment  “+ Transaction” → “+ Incoming”, payee — the client, amount. Tap the “Category” field — “Where to put the income” opens. Choose “Income for December” instead of “Income for November”. Save. The transaction date stays the real one. Only the budget month the money shows up in changes.  Where to start For the first month you'll have to both spend what you have and save for the next one. Start with a payment you haven't assigned yet. Until you have enough for a month ahead, put at least part of it into next month: the app shows how much is already there in “Month budget” on “Overview” — the “December budget” line. The goal is an “Age of money” of 30 days or more: it means you're spending last month's money. More in the article [“Overview”](overview.md#age-month). A cushion for lean months Even with money a month ahead, two lean months in a row happen. A cushion is an envelope that gets you through them.  How to set it up  The “Rainy day fund” category — or one of your own, “Cushion”. A “Balance” goal: the amount is your usual spending for 3–6 months. How much that is — “Average income per month” and “Spending trend”, below. In a good month, put everything above the usual into the cushion. The “Balance” goal makes sure the reserve doesn't melt away: spend part of it, and the app asks you to put it back. More in the article [“Goals”](goals.md#balance).  A lean month There wasn't enough for the envelopes, and spending went into the red. Tap the red amount on “Budget” → “Cover from another category” → on the “Rainy day fund” row, “Take …”. The money moves from the cushion to where the minus is. More in the article [“Budget”](budget.md#screen). Taxes — straight into their own envelope The tax on a payment is easy to spend: the money is on the card, and the tax is due next quarter.  A “% income” goal  The “Taxes” category. A “% income” goal — the percentage you pay. Under the percentage, leave “From this month's income”: tax is calculated on the money that came in, not on the average. Each payment updates the goal by itself: more came in, the goal went up, and “… to go” tells you how much to add. What you set aside builds up in the envelope until the payment date: a plus carries over from month to month. More in the article [“Goals”](goals.md#percent).  Then this month's “% income” goal is known on the 1st: the month's income arrived last month. Handy — the tax is set aside first thing, along with the other envelopes. Money came in — divide it up in one tap Dividing up each payment by hand gets tiring. The “By percentage” auto-assign does it for you.  Set it up once  On “Budget”, tap “unassigned” in the header — “Auto-assign the budget” opens. “By percentage” → “Set percentages”: for example, “Taxes” — 5%, “Rainy day fund” — 20%, “Investments” — 10%. The percentages are remembered. Whatever isn't covered by a percentage stays in “unassigned” — assign it to the month's envelopes yourself. From then on: money came in — tap “unassigned” → “By percentage”. The app divides up exactly what's unassigned right now.  With an irregular income, a fixed amount is impossible one month and laughable the next. A percentage rises and falls along with your income. Rounding — the “To whole”, “To 10”, “To 100” chips on the same sheet. Clients and projects  The client is the payee Record every payment with the client in the “Payee” field. Tap the client in “Settings” → “Payees” — their screen opens: “Income trends” shows how much they pay on average, and the “Year” period shows all their payments for the year. You can see who feeds you and who pays twice a year. More in the article [“Payees and tags”](payees-tags.md#payee).  The project is a tag Create a tag for the project: “cafe website”. Put it on both the client's payment and the project's costs: a service subscription, a taxi to a meeting, a font. The tag screen shows “Spent”, “Received” and “Net” — what the project really brought in. More in the article [“Payees and tags”](payees-tags.md). Expected payments The invoice is out, and the money was promised by the 15th. To not forget and to see what's coming, create a scheduled payment.   “Settings” → “Scheduled payments” → “+ Payment”. “+ Incoming”, the client, the amount, the date payment was promised, “Repeat” — “Once”. The payment appears in “What’s ahead” and in the “Calendar” on “Overview”. The money arrived on time — “Confirm” on the confirmation screen. Earlier than due — swipe the payment row left — “Enter”. The client is late — open the payment and change the “Date” field. Until the payment is confirmed, it isn't in the budget: envelopes don't get filled with promised money. More in the article [“Scheduled payments”](scheduled.md). What to watch   More about the reports in the article [“Reports”](reports.md). Keep work money separate If your work has its own account and its own expenses — services, equipment, an accountant — you can keep them in a **second budget**, for example “Work”. Tap the budget name in the “Overview” header — there's the budget switcher and a new budget. The work budget holds payments and work expenses. What you take for living goes as a transfer to your personal card: in the work budget it's spending, in the personal one it's income. That way your personal budget lives on an even amount every month, and all the ups and downs stay in the work budget.
scenario-paycheck: Paycheck to paycheck The money runs out before the month does, and payday is still a week away. How to divide up what you have, make it to the next paycheck without red, and step by step get out of the rat race. The big idea Envelopes don't give you more money than you have. But they show you **in advance** whether it'll last until payday — not on the last day, but on the first.   Assign only what you have An envelope is filled with money that's already in your accounts. A promised paycheck isn't money yet. [How](#now).  Essentials first Housing, food, getting to work, medicine, a loan payment. Everything else comes after. [How](#now).  A minus isn't failure Move money from another envelope and carry on. [How](#minus). Payday — divide it up right away Until money is divided up, it feels like a lot. Divided into envelopes, it tells the truth: $200 for food until the 5th, and that's it.  In order  Open “Budget”. At the top is “unassigned”: that much money still has no job. First fill the envelopes you can't get to the next paycheck without: rent, utilities, “Groceries”, getting to work, medicine, the minimum loan payment. Then everything else, until “unassigned” reaches zero. Not enough for everything? Some envelopes stay empty. That's not a mistake but an honest answer: there's no money for that this month. How to put money into an envelope — step by step in the article [“Budget”](budget.md#screen).  You handed out more than you have in your accounts. Reduce what's set aside in one of the envelopes — tap the amount and enter less. The money goes back to “unassigned”. Two paychecks a month Money twice a month — you divide it up twice. The first check goes to what's needed until the second. The second goes to the rest and to what comes after it.  Bills before payday — as scheduled payments Create scheduled payments for rent, utilities, your phone: “Settings” → “Scheduled payments” → “+ Payment”. They appear in the “What’s ahead” block and in the “Calendar” on “Overview”, and a reminder arrives the day before they're due. You see which bills come before payday and which after — and what to cover from the first check. More in the article [“Scheduled payments”](scheduled.md). How much you can spend per day  “≈ … a day” Tap a category on “Budget” — its screen opens. Under “Available” is how much you can spend each day until the end of the month without going negative. With $140 in “Groceries” and ten days left in the month — “≈ $14 a day”. More in the article [“Category screen”](category.md#screen).  “Running out” on “Overview” There's still money in the envelope, but you're spending faster than the month is going — the category shows up yellow in the “Running out” block. That's a signal to slow down now, not in a week. More in the article [“Overview”](overview.md#blocks).  “Month spending” A block on “Overview”: whether you're spending more this month than usual by this date. A red minus You spent more than the envelope had — the amount is red. Cover it right away, before the month ends.   Tap the red amount on “Budget”. In the “Overspent” sheet, tap “Cover from another category”. “Where to take the money from” opens: “Unassigned” and every envelope that has money. Tap “Take …” next to an envelope you can spare. The minus is covered — “Overspending covered!”. More in the article [“Budget”](budget.md#screen).  It's reset to zero, but not without a trace: next month's “unassigned” shrinks by the same amount. Your next paycheck ends up smaller by exactly that minus. More in the article [“How the budget works”](start.md#months).  Tap “unassigned” in the “Budget” header → “Cover all overspending”. The app covers all the month's minuses from unassigned money in one go. A credit card isn't the way out The envelope is empty, but the credit card has room. The temptation is understandable, but a credit card purchase from an empty envelope is a **yellow** minus: there's no money, and the debt grows. Next month you'll have to pay it from your new paycheck — which means it'll be smaller again. More in the scenario [“Credit cards and debt”](scenario-credit.md#yellow). Record every day An envelope tells the truth only while all spending is recorded in it. One forgotten purchase from yesterday — and “≈ … a day” is lying to you.   The evening reminder: “Settings” → “Planning” → “Reminders” → “Daily spending” → “Remind me to add spending”. It arrives only if you haven't entered anything that day. **Right after installing:** off. The fastest way to record is at the checkout: [by voice](voice.md) or [with the receipt scanner](receipt.md). No time to pick a category? — [“To inbox”](entry.md#inbox), and sort it out in the evening. How to get out of the rat race The goal isn't just to scrape by, but one day to live on money earned a month ago. Go step by step, one at a time.  A small cushion The “Rainy day fund” category with a “Balance” goal — to start, enough for at least a week of spending. Your phone breaks — the money comes from here, not from the food envelope. More in the article [“Goals”](goals.md#balance).  Irregular expenses — a little at a time Insurance, gifts and shoe repairs stop wrecking the month if you set money aside for them every month. A “By date” goal works out how much. More in the scenario [“Saving up for something big”](scenario-saving.md).  Money a month ahead Every month, leave a little on top. Once you've saved a whole month, record your paycheck for next month: “Category” → “Income for December”. From then on every month is paid for in advance, and payday no longer matters. How much you already have for next month — “Month budget” on “Overview”, the “December budget” line. How it's going — “Age of money”: 30 days or more means you're out of the rat race. More in the article [“Overview”](overview.md#age-month) and in the article [“How the budget works”](start.md#ladder).
scenario-credit: Credit cards and debt A credit card, a car loan, a debt you had before the app. How to set them up, how to pay so the budget doesn't lie, and how to watch the debt shrink. Credit card There's one rule: a purchase on a credit card spends envelope money just like a purchase on a debit card. The difference is where that money waits: not in an account but in the credit card's category, until you pay the bank.  How to set it up  “Accounts” → “⋮” → “Add an account”. Type — “Credit card”. Name — whatever you call the card. Amount — how much you owe the bank right now. Type it and tap “±” to make it negative. Save. The card goes to the “Credit cards” section, and on “Budget” a category with the same name appears in the “Card payments” group. Leave that category alone: the app uses it to count the debt of this particular card. More in the article [“Accounts”](accounts.md#screen).  A purchase Record it as usual: account — the credit card, category — what you bought. You bought groceries for $35 — “Groceries” got $35 thinner, and the same $35 moved into the credit card's category for the payment. You don't need to set anything aside yourself. Debt you had before you started The starting debt — $800 on the card from last year — isn't set aside by the app: there was never money for it in the envelopes.  Set money aside for it in the credit card's category, like any envelope: on “Budget”, tap its amount and enter what you can manage this month. All at once or a little at a time — your call. Until you set it aside, there's no money for paying it off. The yellow minus You spent more on the credit card than the envelope had — the amount turned **yellow**, with a card icon. Red, with a wallet icon, is a minus from your own money.   Red eats your money A minus on a debit card or cash. At the end of the month it reduces next month's “unassigned”.  Yellow grows your debt You didn't spend money — you borrowed it. Only the covered part went into the credit card's category; for the rest, there's no money for the payment.  What to do Cover a yellow minus like a red one: tap the amount → “Cover from another category” → “Take …” from another envelope. Then the money for the payment is topped up automatically. Couldn't do it? Next month, put the difference straight into the credit card's category. Paying the card How much to pay the bank is shown in the credit card's category on “Budget”: that much is already set aside for the payment.   “+ Transaction”, account — your debit card. “Payee” → the “Transfers” section → your credit card. The form header turns gray, and no category is needed. Amount — how much you're paying. Save. The money on your debit card goes down, so does the credit card debt, and with it the amount set aside in the credit card's category. The envelopes don't change: you did the spending earlier, when you made the purchases. More in the article [“Transaction form”](entry.md#transfer).  The credit card's category holds exactly as much as you spent on the card from your envelopes. Pay everything set aside each month, and no new debt builds up. Pay only the minimum, and the rest stays in the category, waiting; the bank charges interest on the remaining debt. Card interest and fees The bank charged interest or a service fee — that's spending.  Record an expense: account — the credit card, payee — the bank, category — one of its own, for example “Interest and fees”. The envelope shrinks, and the money for the payment is set aside, as with any purchase. It shows in the reports too: what this credit costs you. Loan A car loan, a mortgage, an installment plan — money you've already spent and are paying back in parts.  How to set it up  “Accounts” → “⋮” → “Add an account”. Type — “Loan”. Amount — how much is left to repay according to the bank statement, with a minus sign (“±”). The account goes to the “Debts” section. It's off budget: this money has no envelopes, and the budget doesn't touch the starting debt.  An envelope for the payment Create a category for the monthly payment — for example, “Loans” in the “Fixed expenses” group — and a “Monthly” goal for the payment amount. Every month the goal reminds you to set the money aside. More in the article [“Goals”](goals.md#monthly). Paying a loan   “+ Transaction”, account — the card you pay from. “Payee” → “Transfers” → the loan account. The loan is off budget, so the app asks for a category: choose “Loans”. The money leaves the envelope, and the debt on the loan account goes down.  Record the whole payment as a single transfer, as above. Then once a month, record the interest on the loan account itself: “Outgoing”, account — the loan, payee — the bank, amount — the interest. No category needed: the account is off budget. Then the debt in the app matches the bank, and the “Loans” envelope gives up exactly your payment.  Create a scheduled payment as a transfer: “Settings” → “Scheduled payments” → “+ Payment”, “Payee” → “Transfers” → the loan account, category “Loans”, “Repeat” — “Monthly”. The payment appears on both accounts' screens, a reminder arrives in advance, and “Confirm” records the transfer. The same goes for a credit card payment: from your debit card to the credit card. More in the article [“Scheduled payments”](scheduled.md#new). Watching the debt   More about the reports in the article [“Reports”](reports.md#capital).
scenario-saving: Saving up for something big A laptop, a renovation, a car, a down payment on an apartment. How to set aside a little at a time, see whether you'll make it by the deadline, and not spend the savings by accident. An envelope just for the purchase Money for a laptop mixed in with money for living gets spent first. A separate envelope protects it: while it sits in “Laptop”, it doesn't show up in “Groceries”.   On “Budget”, find the group that holds “Big purchases” and “Travel & vacation”. Tap “⊕” next to its name — a new category. Name it after the purchase: “Laptop”. Or save in the ready-made “Big purchases” if there's only one purchase. More in the article [“Budget”](budget.md#screen). A “By date” goal Tell the app how much and by which month — it works out how much to put in each month.   Tap the category on “Budget” → the “Goal” card → “Add a goal”. “Goal type” — “By date”. “Amount” — the price of the purchase, “Save up by month” — when you need it. “Save”. A $2,400 laptop in six months — the goal will ask for $400 a month. Miss a month, and the shortfall is spread over the remaining ones, so the payment grows. Put in more, and the next ones shrink. More in the article [“Goals”](goals.md#bydate).  A “Balance” goal: the envelope should hold this amount, and when doesn't matter. It suits “a new car someday” and an emergency cushion. More in the article [“Goals”](goals.md#balance). Am I on track  A quick estimate on the category screen Tap the category — a “By date” goal has a switch under the bar: “By amount” and “By date”. Move “Save per month” — you see which month you'll get there. Move the month — you see how much to put in. Like the new date? — “Make it the goal date: …”. More in the article [“Goals”](goals.md#card).  Short this month On “Budget”, under the amount there's a flag and “… to go”. The “Underfunded” chip above the list leaves only those categories. On “Overview”, the shortfall shows in the “Goals” and “What’s ahead” blocks. Where the money is Savings are often kept in a separate account: a savings account, a deposit, a piggy bank. How you set up that account decides whether the money stays in the envelope.   On budget — for a purchase An account of the “Bank account” type. You moved $400 from checking to savings — the “Laptop” envelope didn't change: the money moved, but it's still yours and still in the budget. The goal sees it and doesn't ask again. **Saving for a purchase? Choose this option.**  Off budget — for wealth An account of the “Tracking” type: investments, a retirement deposit. The app records a transfer there as money leaving an envelope — it asks for a category, and the envelope empties. This won't work for a purchase: the goal will ask for money again, even though you have it. More in the article [“Accounts”](accounts.md#kinds). Several goals at once A vacation, a laptop and holiday gifts — there may not be enough money for everything this month.  “Budget” → “⋮” → “Assign to goals”. The app spreads “unassigned” across all goals at once. Not enough for everything? Goals get money in order, top to bottom, as the categories are arranged on “Budget”. Keep what matters higher up: “⋮” → “Change the order”. More in the article [“Goals”](goals.md#allocate). The purchase   Record the purchase as usual — in the “Laptop” category. The envelope empties — that's what you were saving for. It came out cheaper? The rest stays in the envelope. Need it elsewhere? On “Budget”, tap the “Laptop” amount and enter less: the difference goes back to “unassigned”. It came out more expensive? The amount turns red. Tap it → “Take …” from another envelope. Don't need the goal anymore? “Budget” → “⋮” → “Goals” → tap the category → “Delete”. The money in the envelope stays. The category with the purchase itself can't be deleted — only hidden.  That works too: the money from “Laptop” is set aside for paying off the card. Bought it on credit or in installments? That's a debt; how to track it is in the scenario [“Credit cards and debt”](scenario-credit.md#loan). How much I save  The “Pay yourself” block on “Overview” shows what percent of your income you set aside — for the month, three months and the year. The norm is 10%. Choose which categories count as “saved” in “Settings → Budget → Pay yourself”: “Big purchases”, “Laptop”, “Rainy day fund”. More in the article [“Overview”](overview.md#blocks).
scenario-trip: A trip with friends You paid for lodging for four, a friend paid for dinner, gas is split in half, and abroad there's cash in another currency on top of that. How to save for a trip, see what it cost, and not lose track of who owes whom. Before the trip  Save in “Travel & vacation” with a “By date” goal: the amount is what you expect to spend, the month is when you're going. The app works out the monthly contribution. More in the scenario [“Saving up for something big”](scenario-saving.md#goal). A tag for the trip Trip spending lands in different categories — “Groceries”, “Transport”, “Travel & vacation”. A tag gathers it together.   On the very first purchase of the trip, open “Additional” → “Tags” → type a name, for example “Tahoe”, → “Create tag “…””. Put this tag on every trip purchase. The tag's “⋮” → “Show in My tags” — the trip total will be on “Overview”. The tag screen shows “Spent” and “By category” — what the trip cost and where the money went. More in the article [“Payees and tags”](payees-tags.md#tag). You pay for everyone You paid for lodging for four: $800. Your share is $200, and the other $600 should come back to you.  Split the amount into your share and your friends' share  Record the $800 purchase, account — your card, tag — “Tahoe”. “Category” → “Split the amount”. The first part is “Travel & vacation”, $200: that's your share. The second part is also “Travel & vacation”, $600, and on it “+ tag” → a new tag “Tahoe: friends owe”. Open the “Tahoe: friends owe” tag screen → “⋮” → “Settle up”. Now the tag screen says “to collect $600”: that's how much you're owed. More about split amounts in the article [“Transaction form”](entry.md#split).  “Settle up” calculates spent minus received. If you turned it on for “Tahoe”, your own share would also hang there as “To collect”, and the settlement would never balance. A tag on just your friends' share comes to zero once everything is paid back. A friend paid you back   “+ Transaction” → “Incoming”. Payee — the friend, amount — how much they paid back, account — where the money arrived. “Category” → “To an expense category…” → “Travel & vacation”. This isn't income — it's your money returning to the envelope. Tags — “Tahoe” and “Tahoe: friends owe”. Once all three have paid you back, the “Tahoe: friends owe” tag screen says “Settled” in green. And for “Tahoe”, “Net” will be $600 less than “Spent” — for lodging, exactly your share remains. More in the article [“Transaction form”](entry.md#refund). A friend paid A friend paid for dinner, and your share is $50. No money has left your card yet — there's nothing to record.  When you pay the friend back, record it then: an expense, payee — the friend, category — “Travel & vacation”, tag — “Tahoe”. Until you pay, keep the debt in your head or in a note — the app doesn't track other people's wallets. Abroad   Paying with your own card The bank charges the money in your card's currency. Record the amount the bank charged — you can see it in the bank's app. The amount in local currency, if you need it, goes in the note: “€42 dinner”.  You took cash in a foreign currency Create a “Cash €” account: “Accounts” → “⋮” → “Add an account”, type “Tracking”, “Account currency” — €. Only an off-budget account can have its own currency. How to work with it is below.  Exchanging and spending cash  You exchanged money — record a transfer from your card to “Cash €”. Under the payee, “Credited” and “Rate” appear: how many euros you got. The account is off budget, so the app asks for a category: “Travel & vacation”. The money left the envelope right at the exchange. Record cash spending in euros on the “Cash €” account — no category needed, the envelope has already paid. Add the “Tahoe” tag as usual. Euros left over and exchanged back? A transfer from “Cash €” to your card, “Category” → “To an expense category…” → “Travel & vacation”. The money returns to the envelope. More about currencies in the scenario [“Several currencies and the exotic”](scenario-currencies.md). After the trip   The “Tahoe” tag screen: “Net” is what the trip cost you after all paybacks, “By category” shows where the money went. Handy when you save for the next one. Spending in euros is on a separate line: there's no conversion at a rate, and the exchange itself is a transfer, so it isn't in “Spent”. Don't need the tag in the picker anymore? The tag's “⋮” → “Hide from picker”. It stays on the transactions. Money left in “Travel & vacation”? Let it sit until the next vacation: a plus carries over from month to month.
scenario-currencies: Several currencies and the exotic Your salary in one currency, savings in another, a little bitcoin and trips abroad. What the app can do with currencies, where the limits are, and how to keep your books so the envelopes don't lie. The main rule **A budget has one currency.** All envelopes, all budget accounts and “unassigned” are in it. Other currencies live in accounts **off budget**: you see how much is there, but that money isn't divided among the envelopes.  An envelope answers “how much can I spend on food”. If it holds both dollars and euros, the answer changes every day along with the exchange rate. One currency in the envelopes — and the answer is always the same. Budget currency  “Settings” → “Budget” → “Budget currency”. The list has sixty currencies, the current one in the first row, with a search by name and symbol at the top: “zloty” finds “Złoty”. Only the symbol changes — the app doesn't convert amounts. If you kept your budget in dollars and pick euros, $1,000 becomes €1,000. That's why you choose the currency at the start, not in the middle of your bookkeeping.  Each budget has its own currency. Living between two countries? You can keep two budgets: “Home” in dollars and “Berlin” in euros. Tap the budget name in the “Overview” header — there's the budget switcher and a new budget; you'll be asked for the currency when creating it. An account in another currency   “Accounts” → “⋮” → “Add an account”. Type — “Tracking” (or “Loan” if it's a debt). Only an off-budget account can have its own currency. In the “Account currency” section, tap the “Currency” field — a list of sixty currencies opens, the same as for the budget: the current one in the first row, a search by name and symbol at the top. Names are in the country's own language: “zloty” finds “Złoty”. Cryptocurrency — chips under the field: ₿, USDT, USDC. Not there? Type it yourself in “Or type your own (ticker)”: ETH, a stock or fund ticker. The account's amounts will be labeled with it. Amount — how much is in the account in that currency. The account goes to the “Off budget” section, with amounts in its own symbol: “€1,200.00”. More in the article [“Accounts”](accounts.md#kinds). Exchange Bought euros with dollars? That's a transfer between your own accounts, just with a rate.   “+ Transaction”, account — your dollar card, “Payee” → “Transfers” → the euro account. Amount — how many dollars left. Under the payee are “Credited” and “Rate”. Enter either the rate or how many euros arrived — the other is calculated. The button next to the rate flips its direction: dollars per one euro or euros per one dollar. The euro account is off budget — the app asks for a category: which envelope the money left. For example, “Rainy day fund” or “Investments”. More in the article [“Transaction form”](entry.md#transfer).  A transfer from the euro account to your card. The “Category” field opens “Where to put the income”: “Income for …” — if it's new money to hand out, “To an expense category…” — if it's returning to the envelope it left. Living in one country, saving in another  The budget is in the currency you're paid in and spend every day: dollars, euros, pounds. Money back home, a deposit in another currency, dollars in a “rainy day” stash — off-budget accounts, each in its own currency. The envelopes count what you live on, and the rest is visible next to them on “Accounts”. Record card spending abroad as the amount the bank charged in your card's currency. The amount in local currency, if you need it, goes in the note. More in the scenario [“A trip with friends”](scenario-trip.md#abroad). Cryptocurrency  An off-budget account, the ₿, USDT or USDC chip under the “Currency” field — and the “Cryptocurrency” switch turns on by itself: “8 decimal places”. For your own ticker (ETH, SOL), turn it on by hand. Picked a regular currency from the list? The switch turns off. The number of decimal places is chosen once: once the account has transactions, the switch says “Cannot change: the account has transactions”. Currencies without cents  The yen, won and dong have no minor units, but the app still shows “.00”. It's only the display: type whole numbers as usual. With “With a decimal point” entry, 1500 is 1,500, not 15.00. How amounts are typed — “Settings” → “Language and formats” → “Amount entry”. How amounts are written  “Settings” → “Language and formats” → “Amount format”: the thousands and decimal separators, the currency symbol on the left or right. Out of the box it follows the interface language: in English, “$1,234.56”. English on a phone from India gets lakhs and crores right away: “₹12,34,567.89”. More in the article [“Settings”](settings.md#formats). What's missing   **Exchange rates from the internet.** You enter the exchange rate yourself, when you exchange. That's also protection: the app doesn't ask any service for rates, so nobody outside learns which currencies your money is in. Your data stays with you — as the [privacy policy](settings.md#s-about) says too. **Conversion into one currency.** “Net worth” adds up only accounts in the budget currency: a euro account isn't included. On “Accounts”, a section that has an account in another currency shows no total — there's no way to add dollars to euros. **Budget accounts in another currency.** Why — [above](#rule).
overview: Overview The first screen at launch: is there enough money, what's urgent and what's ahead — in one feed of cards. Why this screen “Overview” opens first every time you launch the app. It's a morning look at your money: is everything all right, what's running low, what's ahead. You don't divide up money or edit transactions here — that's what “Budget” and “Activity” are for. Here you look and decide where to go next.   Is everything all right Is there unassigned money, where's a minus, which envelopes are emptying faster than the month is going.  What already happened Recent transactions, big expenses, a calendar of spending days.  What's ahead Scheduled payments, goals that are short of money, and this month's spending against the usual. Minimize the app for more than half a minute, and when you come back it opens “Overview” again. If you'd rather return to where you left off, choose that in “Settings → Appearance → Return to”. What's where on the screen Tap any screenshot to open it full screen.    **Settings** — the gear. All of the app's settings: sync, backups, appearance, language. **Budget name** — tap it to open the list of your budgets and switch to another one.  You can have several budgets: for example, personal and family, or an old one you don't want to delete. To create, rename or delete a budget — the “⋮” menu → “Budgets” ([below](#menu)). **Sync** — two arrows in a circle. Tap it — your edits go to the cloud, and edits from other devices come here.  The number on the icon is how many edits haven't been sent yet. Right after a sync the icon flashes for 15 seconds: green — it worked, red — it didn't. Hold your finger on it, and the app tells you what happened. A single failure is usually the network: the subway, a cabin in the woods. If it fails four times in a row, the icon stays red with a “!” inside until it goes through. No cloud connected — the icon is its usual color, with no number. **The “⋮” menu** — budgets, choosing blocks, “Hide amounts”. Explained [below](#menu). **“Unassigned”** — money that's in your accounts but not yet divided among envelopes. Tap it, and the app suggests how to hand it out.  The label changes along with the number:  **“Unassigned”** — there's money to hand out. In the screenshot it's $300: a paycheck arrived, and the envelopes for November are already filled. **“All assigned”**, in green — every dollar has a job. That's the goal. **“Over-assigned”**, in red — more was put into envelopes than there is in the accounts. Take the extra out of some category on the “Budget” screen. You can tap it only when there's something to hand out. The “Auto-assign the budget” sheet opens: “Cover all overspending”, “Underfunded”, “Assigned last month” and other ways. Next to each is how much it would take. Nothing changes until you confirm. More about envelopes — in the article [“Budget”](budget.md). **“Age of money”** — how many days on average your money sits before you spend it.  In the screenshot it's 52 days: what you spend today came to you almost two months ago. The app takes the last ten expenses and looks at which income paid for each — the oldest money gets spent first. Under 30 days — you live paycheck to paycheck, and any delay in pay hits the budget. Over 30 — you're spending last month's money, and the new paycheck calmly waits its turn. A minus — more was spent than there was money in the budget accounts. The hourglass on the icon says the same: full — 30 days or more, half empty — less, empty — a minus. Age can be calculated three ways, and from 30 days it makes sense to live on last month's money. All of that — [below](#age). **Blocks** — summary cards, one under another. Which to show and in what order is up to you. Each block is explained [below](#blocks). **“+ Transaction”** — record spending or income. Above it — the camera (a receipt by QR code) and the microphone (by voice). Scroll down, and the buttons fold into a single “+”.  It's the same form as on the [“Activity”](transactions.md) screen: every tab has a way into it. The blocks in order Under the “Unassigned” chip (callouts 5 and 6) come the cards. Here they're in the order they have right after installing. A block with nothing to show hides itself: no tags — no “My tags”, no goals — no “Goals”. To remove a block, bring it back or move it higher — “⋮” → “Widgets” ([below](#menu)).   Recent transactions The last five entries: date, payee, amount, category and note. Handy for checking that everything from yesterday is recorded.  Income has a “+” sign, spending a “−”. A split amount (“Target” in the screenshot) has a fork icon next to it, and its categories are listed separated by dots. There are two incoming amounts in the screenshot: a paycheck and $43 from Andrew — a friend paid back his half of “Target”. That's not income but a refund to “Groceries” (how to record it — in the article [“Transaction form”](entry.md)). The rows here aren't tappable. To fix a transaction, open [“Activity”](transactions.md).   Overspending and “Running out” Envelopes that need attention right now. Tap a row to open that category's screen.   **“Overspent”**, in red — the category is in the minus: you spent more than you set aside. A wallet icon means a minus from your own money; it will take from next month's “unassigned”. A card icon and yellow mean a minus on a credit card: it grew into card debt rather than eating your money. To clear a minus — on the [“Budget”](budget.md) screen. **“Running out”**, in yellow — the envelope still has enough money, but you're spending faster than the month is going. The app divides the month's plan evenly by days and allows a 15% margin. In the screenshot, today is November 10, and more has been spent on “Groceries” than due by this date, even with the margin. **“All under control”** — no minuses, no warnings. The block shows this instead of being empty. Categories with exactly zero left don't appear here: the plan was met to the cent.   Where the money went The month's five most expensive categories: amount, percent of all spending, and a bar of the same length.  In the screenshot, “Rent” is 76% of November spending: rent is paid on the 1st, all at once, while other spending builds up day by day. By the end of the month the percentages even out. Swipe the card right with your finger to see last month, left for the next one. To get back to the current month — the “Today” chip, which appears in the card's header when you've moved to another month.   What's ahead The nearest scheduled payments and goals that are short of money — up to six rows, by date.  A scheduled payment has a calendar icon, a goal has a flag. There are two goals in the screenshot: “Rainy day fund” is $1,124.53 short by the end of November, “Travel & vacation” — $100. The amount in yellow is how much more needs to go in. The rows aren't tappable: to put money into a category — the [“Budget”](budget.md) screen, scheduled payments — “Settings → Planning”.   Month budget Where the “Unassigned” number came from: a ladder from last month's balance to the total.  Read it top to bottom, like a receipt:  **Carried over from October** — how much wasn't assigned last month. **November budget** — this month's income: in the screenshot, two paychecks of $1,400 each. **Assigned in November** — how much has already been divided among envelopes. **Unassigned** — the total, the same number as on the chip at the top of the screen. Below the line is the “Plan”: how much is already there for December, the average income per month, and how much your goals ask for per month, with the percent of income. Sometimes more rows appear — last month's overspending, money from savings, money set aside ahead; the block hides empty rows. The card can be swiped both ways, forward too: you can assign money for December already in November.   Net worth Everything you own minus debts — and how it changed.  In large type — your net worth today: $12,209.72 in the screenshot. On the right — how much it grew over the period (+$4,343.99 over 6 months), below — a line by month and a breakdown: “Assets” (all accounts with a plus) and “Debts” (credit cards and loans). In the block's “⋮”: the period — 6 months, 12 months, this year or all time — and “Accounts in other currencies”: such accounts appear as separate rows in their own currency, without conversion and outside the overall total. **Right after installing:** the block is off; turn it on in “⋮” → “Widgets”.   Goals How many categories fall short of their goal this month, and by how much. Tap it to open the “Goals” screen.  In the screenshot, two goals are short by $1,224.53 together. Goals are set on the category screen or on the “Goals” screen: “Set aside every month”, “Save up by …”, “Keep on the balance”, “Percent of income” or “list”.   Pay yourself What percent of your income you set aside for your future self — over a month, three months and a year.  The rule is old and simple: from every paycheck, first pay yourself, and only then everyone else. The norm is 10% of income. In the screenshot, 11.2% is set aside in November — $34.00 above the norm. If it's below the norm, the percent has “short” under it, with an amount. Which categories count as “saved” is your choice: “Settings → Budget → Pay yourself”.
