Usually it's savings: “Rainy day fund”, “Investments”. With none selected, there's no block.   Big expenses The month's three biggest expenses — date, payee, amount, category and note.  It helps catch what stands out: an unexpectedly expensive shopping trip is visible right away, not at the end of the month. **Right after installing:** the block is off; turn it on in “⋮” → “Widgets”.   Calendar The month as a grid of days: the brighter the cell, the more was spent. Tap a day to see what happened on it.  A detailed look with the modes and menu — [below](#heatmap).   My tags Up to four tags: how much was spent under them, over what span, and how many transactions.  A tag with “Settle up” shows on the right how much to collect or to return to break even: in the screenshot, “#split” shows “to collect $43.00”: a purchase at “Target” was split with a friend, and he has already paid back half. Tap a tag to open its screen. “All tags ›” at the bottom of the block — the whole list. In the block's “⋮”: “Choose tags…” — which four to show and in what order; and the period — “Total for the whole tag” or “Total for this month”. Choose nothing, and the app shows tags with transactions in the last 30 days by itself. No tags — no block. About tags themselves — in the article [“Activity”](transactions.md).   Month spending How much you've spent since the start of the month — against how much you usually spend by this date.  In large type — spending since the 1st: $1,620.99. On the right — the difference from usual: +$59.87, that is, slightly more than usual. The bright line is this month, the thin one is the usual. “Usually” is the middle of your past months over the last year: one unusually expensive month won't shift it. The card can be swiped like “Where the money went”. The calendar in detail The liveliest block on “Overview”: a whole month on one card. Run your eyes over it — and you see which days were expensive and which passed with no spending at all.    Modes What to color: “Spending”, “Income” or “Scheduled”.   **“Spending”** — six shades. The brightest cell is the month's most expensive day, and each step down is half as much. Brightness answers “how many times cheaper was this day than the most expensive one”. **“Income”** — the same for incoming money, in green. **“Scheduled”** — the days scheduled payments are due. A past day where everything was entered gets a check mark; where a payment was missed, the day number is red. In “Spending” mode, a future day with a scheduled payment is outlined with a dashed line.  The calendar menu Three dots in the card's header, to the right of the month. It sets what else to draw on the grid and what to show in the day sheet.  **The day sheet** isn't a menu item. It opens when you tap a number in the calendar grid: a list of what happened that day slides up from the bottom (screenshot [below](#day)). The menu only sets up what that sheet contains. Items in “Spending” mode:  **“Income as dots”** — a day when money came in gets a green dot in its cell. **“Whole day in the day sheet”** — tap a number, and the day sheet shows not only spending but also that day's income: as a collapsed row at the bottom; tap it to expand. Off — the sheet shows only spending. In “Scheduled” mode the items are different: show future payments as a cell fill or a dot, and whether to highlight in red the number of a day with a missed payment. **Right after installing**, “Income as dots” and “Whole day in the day sheet” are off.  Today Today is outlined.  Swipe the calendar with your finger to see another month, back and forward with no limit: it doubles as a regular calendar where you can see which weekday a date falls on. To get back — the “Today” chip in the card's header.  Days without spending How many days of the month passed without a single expense. On the right — the brightness scale.  An empty cell in the past is a day without spending. If the only thing that day was a refund from a store, there's an empty ring instead of a fill. The day sheet: tap a number in the calendar A sheet slides up from the bottom: the date and the day's total in the header, and below it each transaction. A split amount is shown in parts: in the screenshot, “Target” — $61 for groceries and $25 for cleaning supplies.   How to open it: on “Overview”, find the “Calendar” and tap the number of the day you want — in the screenshot above that's the 10th, outlined as “today” (G). The sheet shows what the calendar colors: in “Spending” mode — the day's spending, in “Income” — incoming money. To see both at once, turn on “Whole day in the day sheet” in the calendar menu (F). To close the sheet, swipe it down or tap outside it. In “Scheduled” mode the sheet is different: what isn't entered, what is, and what's still ahead. Swipe a due date left — “Enter”, right — “Delete”. Age of money in detail The number on the chip answers the question: how many days did my money sit before I spent it. Your paycheck came on October 1, and on November 5 you buy bread with what's left of October's money — that money is 35 days old. The app takes the last ten expenses, finds for each which income paid for it (the oldest money first), and shows the average.   Under 30 days Paycheck to paycheck: today's spending is paid from the latest paycheck, and any delay hits right away.  30 or more A month ahead: you spend last month's money. That's the method's goal — [what to do next](#age-month).  A minus More was spent than there was in the budget accounts. Three ways to calculate Age of money is a debatable metric, and there's no single correct formula for it. So the way is up to you: “Settings → Budget → Age of money”. The number changes right away — both on the chip and in the “Age of money” report.  Classic (YNAB FIFO) · right after installing The YNAB way. It doesn't see transfers at all — neither to savings nor from them. Spending you had no money for weighs exactly −1 day, whether it's a hundred dollars or ten thousand. Good if you don't touch your savings: then it's honest and matches YNAB. Bad if you live on transfers from savings: money arrives in checking, it doesn't see it, and it draws cheerful positive days. On a real budget, the accounts were $3,000 in the minus, covered by transfers from “Investments” — and Classic showed +10 days.  Savings-aware · closest to the truth A transfer from savings is money entering the budget, a transfer to savings is money leaving it. Spending beyond what you had is measured in days of your income: spent a week's income beyond what you had — about minus 7 days. The result is the average over the last 10 expenses, so one expense in the minus among covered ones is softened.  Savings-aware, with debt depth The same as the previous one while the budget is in the plus. But while it's in the minus, it shows not the average but the depth of the hole: how many days of your usual income it will take to close it. That's no longer an age but an alarm signal. Handy while you're climbing out of the minus: the number honestly shrinks with every paycheck. Which to choose Closest to the truth is **“Savings-aware”**: it counts exactly the money in your budget accounts, with everything that came from savings and went to them. Classic is honest only while you don't touch savings. Debt depth is for those who are in the minus right now and want to see how much is left. If you don't move money to savings and back and don't spend more than you have, all three show the same number. Age of 30 days or more: live on last month's money Since your spending is already paid for by the last paycheck, this month doesn't need the current one. Give it straight to the next month: then every month starts with money ready, and you assign it in advance instead of waiting for payday.  How to do it  Record the paycheck as usual: “+ Transaction” → “Incoming”, payee, amount. Tap the “Category” field. The “Where to put the income” sheet opens. Choose “Income for December” — next month — instead of “Income for November”. Save. The transaction date stays the real one — the day the money arrived. Only the budget month it shows up in changes. A paycheck you've already recorded is moved the same way: open it and change the category.  Which paycheck to start with The one you haven't divided among envelopes yet. Moving it reduces this month's “unassigned” by the paycheck amount. If after that it shows a red “Over-assigned”, that money is already working this month: return the paycheck to this month and move the next one.  How the budget changes  **This month** lives on what came in before. The new paycheck no longer lands in its “unassigned”. **Next month** gets its money in advance. On the “Budget” screen, flip forward with the “›” arrow — the paycheck is already in its “unassigned”, and you can fill the envelopes before the 1st. On “Overview”, in “Month budget” below the line — the “December budget” row. **On the 1st** the whole month is already paid for. Money is assigned once, at the start of the month, rather than in bits after every payment. “Assigned last month” in auto-assign does it in one tap. **“% income” goals** based on the month's income are known from the first day: the month's income arrived last month. **Reports** (“Income and expenses”, “Pay yourself”) count such a paycheck in the month it's set aside for. **The age of money itself** doesn't grow from this mark: it grows when you spend less than you earn. The mark locks in the reserve — next month's money won't dissolve into this one. Until its month comes, such income doesn't count toward the age. The “⋮” menu Budgets, how “Overview” looks, and display mode.    Budgets Everything about budgets on one sheet.  “Create a new budget”, “Select a budget”, “Delete the budget”. The last remaining budget can't be deleted — the app needs at least one. To simply switch to another budget, it's faster to tap the name at the top of the screen.  Widgets Which blocks to show on “Overview” and in what order.  A check mark — the block is shown, empty — hidden. To move a block higher or lower, drag it by the handle on the right. The setting lives on this device: on a tablet, “Overview” can look different than on the phone.  Hide amounts Dots instead of numbers. For the moment when someone else can see the screen.  Turned the phone toward someone, taking a screenshot for support, recording a video — turn it on, and amounts on all screens become “••••”. The “+” or “−” sign stays: it says which way the money went, but not how much. Bars, charts and colors stay as they were. While the mode is on, there's a crossed-out eye in the “Overview” header — tap it to bring the amounts back. Or in the same “⋮” — the item is now called “Show amounts”. The mode survives an app restart.  Hints All of this screen's hints in one place.  Help Center This article on the website: it opens in your browser, in the app's language.   What you can do on the screen Most rows on “Overview” are read-only. The ones that can be tapped are those that lead somewhere.
budget: Budget Your envelopes. This is where you decide how much money to set aside for food, rent and everything else — and see how much is left in each envelope. Why this screen Picture a stack of envelopes labeled “Groceries”, “Rent”, “Utilities”. On payday you divide money among them. When you spend, you take it out of the right envelope. An envelope is empty — there's no more money for that this month, unless you move some over from another one. The “Budget” screen is that stack of envelopes. Each row is an envelope (in the app it's called a category), and the amount on the right is how much is in it now. There's one main rule: hand out all your money to envelopes until “All assigned” appears at the top.   Divide up a paycheck Money came in — “unassigned” appeared at the top. Hand it out to the envelopes.  Check before buying “Can I afford new sneakers?” — look at the amount next to “Clothing & shoes”.  Clear the red Spent more than you set aside? Move money over from another envelope. What's where on the screen Tap any screenshot to open it full screen.    **Month** — which month you're dividing up right now.  The “‹” and “›” arrows flip through months. Tap the name to open a month picker, so you don't have to flip one at a time. You can go forward without limits — and that's useful: in September you can already set money aside for December gifts. Each month has its own envelopes, and whatever's left in an envelope moves to the next month by itself. **“Unassigned”** — money that isn't in any envelope yet. The most important number on the screen.  A paycheck arrives — it lands here. Your job is to hand it out to envelopes until this reaches zero. This spot has three states:  **a number on a colored chip** — the money is waiting for a job. Tap the chip to open auto-assign: the app offers to divide the money like last month, by average spending, by goals or by your percentages; **“✓ All assigned”** — goal reached: every dollar has a job. As in the screenshot; **red “over-assigned”** — you've put more into envelopes than you have. Tap it — and take the extra out of envelopes. **The “⋮” menu** — goals, order, how rows look. Each item is explained [below](#menu). **Filter chips** — show only the envelopes that need attention.  “Overspent” — envelopes in the minus. “Underfunded” — envelopes still short of this month's goal. “Available” — where there's money. The number on a chip is how many such envelopes there are; in the screenshot, two are waiting for money to reach their goal, and ten have money. A chip with zero isn't shown: if nothing is overspent, “Overspent” simply doesn't appear. Tap “All” to bring back the whole list. **Group** — a shelf of similar envelopes.  “Fixed expenses”, “Everyday expenses”… On the right — how much is in all of this group's envelopes. Tap the name to collapse the group out of the way. Press and hold for a menu: rename, add a category or a new group, delete. Turn on “Percent of income” in the “⋮” menu — and under the group's amount you'll see what percent of the month's income you put into all its envelopes together. You can see right away that “Fixed expenses” take, say, half your paycheck, and “Everyday expenses” get a third. The percent counts every envelope in the group, even if the group is collapsed or some envelopes are hidden by a filter. **⊕ next to a group** — a new envelope in this group. **Category** — one envelope.  Tap the row to open the [category screen](category.md): all spending from this envelope for the month and trends over past months. You can swipe the row left or right with your finger — to rename it, move it to another group or delete it. How exactly — in the section [“What you can do with a row”](#gestures). **The amount on the right** — how much is in the envelope now. Its color is the screen's main hint.   **Green** — there's money, you can spend. **Gray 0.00** — the envelope is empty. For rent you've already paid, that's normal. **Red, with a wallet icon** — you spent more than there was. This minus will eat next month's money. **Yellow, with a card icon** — also a minus, but you paid with a credit card: your card debt grew, and the budget's money wasn't touched. How to put money into an envelope  Tap the amount on the right. A dialog with a keypad opens. It shows not the balance but how much you've already set aside in this envelope this month. Type the new amount — the first digit replaces the old one. Want to add to it instead? Tap “+”, type 35 and “=”. The envelope has a goal? Tap “To goal: …” — the needed amount fills in by itself. Tap “Done”. The money comes from “unassigned” at the top — it goes down by exactly the same amount. How to clear a red minus  Tap the red amount. The “Overspent: Groceries” sheet opens with two items. “Change the budget” opens the amount keypad for this envelope, to top it up from “unassigned”. “Cover from another category” moves money from other envelopes; more on that below. Tap “Cover from another category”. At the top — “To cover: $35”, below — “Where to take the money from”: the first row is “Unassigned”, then every envelope that has money, with each one's balance. Each row has a “Take …” button: the app has already worked out how much can be taken from there. Tap it next to an envelope you can spare. For example, “Fun & hobbies”. A keypad opens with that amount. Agree — tap “Take …”. Want to take less? Type your own amount. One envelope wasn't enough? Take the rest from the next. When the minus is cleared, the sheet says “Overspending covered!”. **Bar** — how much of what you set aside has been spent.  For “Utilities” in the screenshot the bar is almost full: nearly everything set aside for the month is gone. Go past the end, and the bar turns red. If the envelope has a goal, the bar no longer shows spending but how far the goal is met. You can turn bars off in the “⋮” menu. In the current month the spending bar has a thin vertical line — today: how much of the month has gone by. If the fill has passed the line, you're spending faster than the month is going, and the envelope may not last to the end of the month. A goal bar has no such line. **“… of … spent”** — this month's spending against what you set aside this month.  “$92.74 of $100.00 spent” for “Utilities”: you set aside $100, spent $92.74. So why does the right side say 29.44 and not 7.26? Because the envelope also held money from past months — the balance moves along with the envelope. For the same reason “Groceries” has a red line — “$133.28 spent over $400.00” — while the amount on the right is green: the month's plan was exceeded, but the reserve from past months covered the overspending. The envelope is in the plus, all is well. **Goal flag** — “Reached” or “… to go”.  A goal tells an envelope how much it should hold: “$400 for groceries every month” or “$1,300 for vacation by July”. The flag under the amount shows whether the goal is met this month, and if not, how much more to add. Goals are set on the category screen. **“Today”** — go back to the current month. It appears when you've moved to another one. **New spending** — the same three buttons as on “Activity”. [More in the article “Activity”](transactions.md) The “⋮” menu Goals, envelope order, and what to show in the rows.    Goals All the budget's goals on one screen. More in the article [“Goals”](goals.md).  You see which envelopes are on track and which are short. Tap a goal to change it.  Assign to goals Top up each envelope by as much as it's short of its goal. More in the article [“Goals”](goals.md).  The app takes money from “unassigned” and hands it to envelopes with goals — each exactly what's missing. First it shows the plan: what goes where — and only after your “yes” does it assign. If all of the month's goals are already met, it shows how much each one holds — so you can see why there's nothing to hand out.  Change the order Rearrange envelopes and groups.  Handles appear on the rows — drag them. It's handy to keep your most-used envelopes at the top. When you're done, the same menu item is called “Finish sorting”.  Progress bars Show a bar and a “… of … spent” line under each envelope.  Turn them off if you want a short list: just names and amounts remain. Envelopes with a goal always keep their bar — it shows the goal. **Right after installing:** on.  Percent of income What percent of the month's income you set aside in each envelope.  A label like “12%” appears next to the amount: rent eats 40% of income, groceries 15%. Each group shows its own total percent under its amount, across all its envelopes. Spending doesn't change the percent — only how much you set aside and the month's income itself. **What the percent is counted from.** Not from all the money you hand out, but from the “November budget” line in the “Month budget” card on “Overview”: the income assigned to this month. “Carried over from October” isn't part of it. Hand out last month's leftover too, and the percentages come out higher than they really are, and together they can go over 100%. How much of what you assigned is this month's income and how much is the leftover — you can see in the same card ([“Overview”](overview.md#blocks)). **Right after installing:** off. **See also:** the “By percentage” auto-assign — tap “unassigned”.  Hidden categories Envelopes you've put out of sight.  An envelope that has spending can't be deleted — reports need its history. You can hide it: it disappears from the list, and past spending stays. Here you can bring hidden envelopes back.  Hints All of this screen's hints in one place.  Help Center This article on the website: it opens in your browser, in the app's language. What you can do with a row There are no “edit” and “delete” buttons in the row. Instead, you swipe the envelope's row sideways with your finger — to a button that appears from underneath. The first row of the list shows you once how it looks.   Envelopes in the “Card payments” group can't be swiped: the credit card itself manages them, and money is set aside in them automatically.
goals: Goals How much money each envelope needs — and how much more to put in this month. Why goals An envelope answers “how much is in here”. A goal answers “how much should be in here”. The app compares the two and tells you how much more to put in.   **“Food takes $400 a month”** — a “Monthly” goal on “Groceries”. Every month the app reminds you to set aside that $400.  **“Vacation in March, I need $2,000”** — a “By date” goal. The app splits the amount across the months by itself: this much in November, this much in December.  **“The rainy day fund should hold $4,000”** — a “Balance” goal. Spend part of it, and the app asks you to put it back. The goal itself doesn't move money: it only counts. You put the money into the envelope — on the “Budget” screen or with a single “Assign to goals” button (more on it [below](#allocate)). Each category has one goal. What's where on the screen The “Goals” screen opens from “Budget”: “⋮” → “Goals”. It has all the categories with their goals for the selected month. The screenshot shows November in the demo budget: five goals of five kinds.    **Month** — the “‹ ›” arrows flip through months, tapping the name opens a month picker. Goals are calculated for this month. Leave the current one, and a “Today” button appears at the bottom.  **The “⋮” menu** — which categories to show, progress bars, hints — [below](#menu).  **Summary** — “Total” is how many goals there are. “Monthly cost” is how much all goals need this month. “Short” is how much hasn't been put in yet.  **Group** — the same groups as on “Budget”. Under the name — how many goals the group has and how short they are, or “all covered”. Tapping collapses the group.  **A category without a goal** — “no goal”. Tap the row or the “⊕” — “New goal” opens.  **A category with a goal** — the whole goal in three lines. Tapping opens it for editing.  The first line: the category name, the kind of goal (“per month”, “by date”, “balance”, “% income”, “list”) and the goal amount. The second: a bar — how much is done — and the state: a green flag and “Reached”, or a flag and “… to go” — how much to add. The third: the goal's condition in words and the percent done. In the screenshot, “Groceries” is reached: $400 is already set aside in the envelope in November. And “Travel & vacation” is $100 short this month — that's how much is needed per month to reach $2,000 by March. The “⋮” menu    Which categories to show “All categories”, “With goals only” or “Underfunded” — those whose goal is short of something this month. The choice is remembered; if not everything is shown, a dot lights up on the “⋮”.  Progress bars whether to show bars and percentages. Without them the row is shorter, while the goal and amount stay in place.  Hints this screen's hints as a list.  Help Center This article on the website: it opens in your browser, in the app's language. How to set a goal You set a goal here, on “Goals”, or on the category's own screen — with the “Add a goal” button in the “Goal” card. It's the same sheet.      Tap a category without a goal. “New goal” opens. “Goal type” — tap it and pick one of the five. Each says under its name what it's for. Which to use when — [below](#types). “Amount” — tap it and type on the app's keypad. For “% income” there's “Percent of income” instead of an amount, and for “List” — the list's lines. “By date” also has “Save up by month” — the month by which you need the whole amount. “Save”. Until the amount is set, the button is gray.  **Edit or delete** — tap a category with a goal — “Edit the goal” opens with the same fields. At the bottom — “Delete” and “Save”. A deleted goal goes away; the money in the envelope stays.  **A suggestion from scheduled payments** — if the category has a scheduled payment, the goal card on the category screen shows “From the scheduled payment: …”. A payment every month suggests “per month” for its amount; once a year — “save … by the payment”. Five kinds of goal The kind of goal is the rule the app uses to work out “how much is needed this month”. Below, each rule with an example from the screenshot. “Monthly” — for what you spend every month  **How it's calculated** — every month you need to set aside the same amount. The goal looks at how much you put into the envelope **this month**, not at how much is left in it.  “Groceries”, $400 a month. Put $400 in for November — the goal is “Reached”, even if half is already spent. Spending is exactly what this money is for. Put in $270 — “$130 to go”. For groceries, internet, transport, subscriptions. “By date” — save an amount by a certain month    **How it's calculated** — how much is still missing from the whole amount is divided by the remaining months, counting this one. That gives the month's contribution.  “Travel & vacation”, $2,000 by March. At the start of November the envelope holds $750, so $1,250 is missing. Until March, counting November, there are five months — $250 a month. In November $150 is already set aside — the goal says “$100 to go”. Skip a month, and the shortfall is spread over the remaining ones, so the contribution grows by itself. Put in more, and the next contributions shrink. The bar shows something else: how much of the whole amount is already in the envelope. In the screenshot — 45%.  **What for** — a vacation, insurance once a year, holiday gifts, a spring renovation — everything that doesn't happen every month but is predictable. “Balance” — keep a reserve  **How it's calculated** — the envelope should always hold this amount. However much is missing at the start of the month, that's what the goal asks for.  “Rainy day fund”, $4,000. The envelope has $2,875.47 now — the goal asks for “$1,124.53 to go”. There's no deadline: top it up when you can. Took some of the reserve for a repair? The goal asks you to put it back again. For an emergency fund, a medicine cabinet, a car repair reserve. “% income” — set aside a percent of income    **How it's calculated** — the month's goal is your percent of income. The app shows the amount right in the sheet: “Income for November: $2,800.00 · Goal for the month: $280.00”.  **“From this month's income”** — calculated from money that has **already arrived**. The first part of your pay arrived — one goal; the second arrived — the goal grew. While there's no income in the month, the goal is zero and counts as met. **By default:** this one is selected.  **“From average income”** — the average income over the last 12 months. The goal is known from the 1st and doesn't change during the month — handy if you get paid at the end of the month.  **What for** — “set aside 10% of everything I earn” — investments, savings, donations. “List” — what to buy this month A goal made of lines: write down what the category's money will go to this month — and the goal amount adds up by itself. Each month has its own list.      **Lines** — choose “List” in “Goal type”, and the month's lines appear right in the sheet. “⊕ Add a line” — a name and an amount. At the bottom — “Goal for November”: the total of all lines. Until there are lines, “Save” is gray.  **On the category screen** — the lines live in the “Goal” card under the bar. That's where you work with them: tap a line to edit it, swipe left — “Enter”, swipe right — “Delete” (with “Undo” in the message at the bottom).  **“Enter”** — opens the regular transaction form: the planned amount (correct it to the real one), this category, the line's name in the note. Once saved, under the line in green: “✓ recorded $43.00 · Nov 12”, while the planned amount stays on the right: in the screenshot, the cake was planned at $40 and bought for $43.  You can record a line again: one purchase can take several payments — tyres, then fitting. The form fills in what is left of the plan, and the line shows the total of all records and their number. The line's sheet has a link to each transaction and “Record transaction”; the “Reduce to …” button makes the plan equal to what you recorded. A recorded line can't be moved to another month.  **Move to another month** — press and hold a line to turn on selection. Check the ones you want; at the bottom — their total and “⋮”: “Move to December”, “Move to another month…”, “Delete”.  **A new month** — the list is empty: “The list for December is empty” and a “Copy lines from November · amount” button: last month's lines are copied (without the “recorded” marks), and last month doesn't change. The “Goal” card on the category screen Tap a category on “Budget” — [its screen](category.md) opens. Its “Goal” card shows the goal for the screen's month and tells you how much to put in.    **Header** — the goal's description and a pencil to edit. Below — a bar and “Assign … more this month” or “The month goal is met”.  **“By amount” / “By date” estimate** — for a “By date” goal, under the bar: what if you set aside more or less? “By amount”: move the “Save per month” slider — “Save up by month” under it shows when you'll get there, and the line below says “… mo. before the deadline”, “… mo. after the deadline” or “Right on time”. “By date”: move “Save up by month” — under the slider you see how much to set aside per month. Need an exact amount? Tap “Save per month” and type it on the keypad.  The estimate doesn't save anything: leave the screen, and everything is as it was. Like the new date? Tap “Make it the goal date: …”, and the goal takes it. In the screenshot: putting in $400 a month, the vacation money is ready in February — a month before the deadline.  **No goal** — the card has a single button, “Add a goal”. If there's a scheduled payment, a “From the scheduled payment: …” suggestion appears next to it. Assign to goals Your paycheck arrived — divide it among all the goals with one button. “Budget” → “⋮” → “Assign to goals”.    **What it does** — takes money from “unassigned” and puts it into the envelopes whose goals are short of something this month. First it shows the plan — how much goes to which envelope; “Assign” does it, “Cancel” changes nothing.  **If there isn't enough for everything** — goals are covered in order, top to bottom, as the categories are arranged on “Budget”, and the last one gets what's left. In the screenshot, $230 was enough for “Gifts & holidays” and “Travel & vacation” in full, while “Rainy day fund” got $25 of $1,124.53. Keep what matters higher up — the order is changed on “Budget”: “⋮” → “Change the order”.  **If there's nothing to assign** — “unassigned” is empty — the app says so. No goals — it tells you where to set them. All goals are already met — it shows for each how much is set aside and how much is needed.  **The same in auto-assign** — tap “unassigned” in the “Budget” header — the “Underfunded” mode does the same thing. And the category amount calculator on “Budget” has a “To goal: …” button — it fills in exactly what's missing. Where else goals show up A goal isn't visible only here.  **“Budget”** — a category with a goal has a flag under its amount: “Reached” or “… to go”, and the bar shows the goal rather than spending. The “Underfunded” chip above the list leaves only the categories whose goals are short of something. More in the article [“Budget”](budget.md).  **“Overview”** — the “Goals” block shows how many goals there are, how many are met and how much more is needed this month. More in the article [“Overview”](overview.md).
category: Category screen One envelope in full: how much it held, how much was set aside and spent, how much is left and how many days it will last. Also the goal, a note, spending in past months and all of the month's transactions. Why this screen On “Budget”, a category has one row and one number. Here is everything behind it.   Will it last until the end of the month “Available” and under it “≈ … a day”: how much you can spend each day until the end of the month without going negative.  Where the money went All of this category's transactions for the month, by day. Tap any one to open its card.  How much you really need “Spending trends” shows how much usually goes out per month. If you set aside less, every month ends in a minus. How to open it  **“Budget”** — tap a category row. The screen opens on the month selected on “Budget”. That's with the phone upright: in landscape, tapping a table row opens the amount calculator, and on a tablet it opens a panel on the right ([below](#tablet)). **“Overview”** — tap a row in the “Overspent” or “Running out” block. **“Reports”** — tap a list row in “Where the money went” or a tile in “Deviation”. The screen opens on the report's month. What's where on the screen The screen scrolls: the summary at the top, then the “Goal”, “Note” and “Spending trends” cards, and below them the month's transactions. Tap a screenshot to open it full screen.    **Name** — the category's name. Rename it in the “⋮” menu. **“⋮”** — hide, rename or move to another group, delete. Details — [below](#menu). **Month** — “‹ ›” flip through months: past and future, with no limit. Details — [below](#months). **“From …”** — how much was left in the envelope from last month. **“Planned for …”** — how much you set aside in this envelope this month. In small print under the amount — what percent of the month's income that is. **“Spent in …”** — how much left the envelope this month, after refunds. **“Available”** — how much is in the envelope now. The same number as in the category row on “Budget”. **“≈ … a day”** — how much you can spend per day until the end of the month. Only in the current month and only if “Available” is above zero. **“Goal”** — the category's goal for this month: how much more to set aside. More in the article [“Goals”](goals.md#card). **“Note”** — your own text about this category. Details — [below](#note). **“Spending trends”** — how much goes out on average per month. Details — [below](#trends). **Date** — the month's transactions by day, newest at the top. Details — [below](#ops). **Transaction** — a row like in “Activity”, just without the category: there's only one here. **“+ Transaction”** — a new transaction with the category already chosen in the form. The summary: where the numbers come from The summary's four rows add up to one formula:  **“From …”** + **“Planned”** − **“Spent”** = **“Available”**  A plus carries over to the next month, a minus doesn't Didn't spend it all? The rest stays in the envelope and shows up next month in the “From …” row. Spent more than there was? This month “Available” is red. When the month turns over, the minus is reset: next month “From …” will be 0.  Where the reset minus goes depends on how you paid. With cash or a debit card, it reduces next month's “unassigned”. With a credit card, it became card debt. More in the article [“Budget”](budget.md).  Percent of income Under “Planned” — what percent of the month's income you set aside in this envelope. The same percent as in the “Percent of income” badge on “Budget”. No income in the month — no percent. It's counted from the “… budget” line of the “Month budget” card — without last month's leftover; why the percent can then look too high — in the article [“Budget”](budget.md#income-share).  “≈ … a day” “Available” is divided by the days left until the end of the month, today included, and rounded down — so a day never gets more than there is. Spent less today? Tomorrow the number grows. Note Write what belongs in this category, what you're saving for, what you agreed on — anything that will help six months from now. Tap the “Add a note for the category…” field and type: the note saves by itself, there's no button. With a cloud, it reaches your other devices. “Spending trends” How much usually goes out of this category. It counts the 12 full months before this one; the current month isn't included because it isn't over yet. Spending is after refunds.    **“Average monthly spending”** — how much goes out on average per month, counting months with no spending too. That's how much is worth setting aside every month so the envelope doesn't go negative.  **“Average in an active month”** — the average only over months with spending. It appears when there wasn't spending every month: in the screenshot, “Big purchases” has $480 in a month with a purchase, and $96 on average across every month.  **“Spent in …”** — how much went out last month: compare it with this one.  **Percentages under the amounts** — what percent of income that is: for the averages, of the average income over the same months; for last month, of its income. The month's transactions All of this category's transactions for the screen's month, by day: newest at the top. For a split amount, only its part with this category is shown — in the screenshot, “Target”.   The order of transactions within a day and the day total next to the date are set in “Activity”: “⋮” → “Sorting” and “Daily total”. They're the same here. Another month “‹” and “›” above the summary flip through months. Leave the current month, and “Today” appears at the bottom left: tap it to return to the current month.    In a past month you see how much there was and how much was spent then. There's no “≈ … a day” row there: the month is over. In a future month you see how much is already set aside ahead. The “⋮” menu    “Hide the category” The category disappears from “Budget” and from the category list in the transaction form. The money and transactions stay, and it counts in the calculations as before. To bring it back — right here: the item becomes “Show the category”. Or “Budget” → “⋮” → “Hidden categories”.  “Edit the category” A sheet with the name and a “Group” field. Details — [below](#edit).  “Hints” This screen's hints — including the ones you've already closed.  “Help Center” This article on the website: it opens in your browser, in the app's language.  “Delete the category” Only if the category has no transactions at all. Then, after the question “Delete the category?”, it disappears, its goal too, and everything set aside in it goes back to “unassigned”.  If there are transactions, the app says “Cannot delete — there are transactions” and offers “Hide”. A deleted category would vanish from history, and its transactions would be left without an envelope. Rename and move to another group     “Name” The category's new name. The transactions, goal and money stay with it.  “Group” Tap it to open the list of groups. Pick another one and tap “Save”: the category moves to the end of that group together with its money and history.  Categories in the “Card payments” group don't have this field: the app manages their group.  “Delete” The same as “Delete the category” in the menu.  How to move a category to another group  Open the category: “Budget” → tap its row. “⋮” → “Edit the category”. Tap the “Group” field and pick a group. “Save”. You can do the same right on “Budget”: swipe the category row left → “Edit”. On a tablet On a tablet in landscape, tapping a “Budget” row doesn't take you away from the table: the category's summary, goal, note, trends and transactions appear on the right. The month there is the same as the table's; it has no arrows of its own. The panel has no “⋮” menu. To hide, rename or delete a category, use its screen: turn the tablet upright and tap the row, or open the category from “Overview” or from “Reports”.
transactions: Activity The whole history of your money as one feed. Every purchase, every paycheck, every “moved some from checking to savings”. Why this screen The “Budget” screen answers the question “how much more can I spend”. “Activity” answers “so where did it actually go”. It's your diary: everything you've recorded is here by day, the most recent day at the top.   Find “How much was that dinner in March?” — a couple of letters in the search, and there it is.  Fix Wrong category, an extra zero, a duplicate entry — swipe the row and fix it.  Reconcile with the bank Mark what has already gone through on the card — and you immediately see what the bank hasn't processed yet. What's where on the screen Tap any screenshot to open it full screen.    **Search** — finds anything by a couple of letters, an amount or dates.  Type “whole” — the feed keeps only your trips to Whole Foods. It searches everywhere: payee, category, note and amount. “47.55” finds that amount, “milk” finds the note “Milk, eggs, bread”. The search understands dates the way you write them:  **8/15/2026** — a single day; **8/15** — that day in any year: “what did I buy on past birthdays?”; **8/2026** — all of August; **8/2/26-8/10/26** — from and to, both days included. Works with months too: **6/2026-8/2026** — the whole summer. Between “from” and “to”, a hyphen, a dash or a space will do — the app works out where the boundary is. A plain number, like “8”, isn't treated as a date: otherwise a search for $8 would drown in all of August. A hash sign turns on tag search: “#vac” — everything tagged “vacation”, “#vac cafe” — only cafes from the vacation. Two tags separated by a space — transactions that have both. **Payees and tags** — who you pay most often and how much.  A separate screen with two tabs. “Payees” — everyone you've paid and who's paid you, with a total for this year (the period changes in the “⋮” menu). This is often where you find out that the “small” trips to the corner store added up to a vacation over the year. “Tags” — your labels across categories: “vacation”, “renovation”, “gift for mom”. Tap a payee or a tag to open its history. [The article “Payees and tags”](payees-tags.md) **The “⋮” menu** — everything that changes how the feed looks. Each item is explained [below](#menu). **Transaction type** — only expenses, only income, with one tap.  Want to see only money coming in? Tap “Income”. “Transfers” are when money just moved between your own accounts: from checking to savings, to pay off a credit card. “Notes” are entries without an amount, reminders to yourself. Tap the same chip again, and the whole feed comes back. **Date** — jump to any day.  Scrolling six months back with your finger is an acquired taste. Tap the date chip, pick a day in the calendar — and the feed is already there. To get back to today, use the “Today” button at the bottom left. **Flag** — a colored bookmark for yourself.  A flag doesn't calculate anything — it's just a bookmark. Red — “check it wasn't charged twice”, green — “a friend promised to pay me back”. You make up the colors and their meaning. You can set a flag in the transaction form, or on a dozen rows at once through selection. A gray outline means “no flag”. The flag's shape — a dot, a triangle or a wavy flag — is in “Settings → Appearance”. **Category** — which envelope the money left.  A category is an envelope on the “Budget” screen. A purchase at Whole Foods with the “Groceries” category shrinks the groceries envelope: that's how the budget knows how much you still have for food. Was the receipt for both food and cleaning supplies? You can split the amount: each part goes to its own envelope, and the row shows a chip for each part. And for a paycheck, instead of a category there's “Available this month”: the money arrived and is waiting for you to hand it out to envelopes. **Account** — where it was charged from or where it arrived.  Checking, cash, a credit card — each account has its own icon and color, so you recognize it without reading. A transfer has two rows, one for each account: in one the money left, in the other it arrived. That's why a transfer's title shows not a store but the other account: “Visa” on checking, “Checking” on the Visa. **Cleared** — whether it matches the statement. Optional.  You recorded a purchase right at the checkout, and the bank processed it a day or two later. The circle keeps you from getting confused: empty — the bank doesn't have this transaction yet, a check mark — it does. Saw the purchase in your bank's app? Tap the circle. Once a month you can reconcile the whole account. Then the check marks turn into locks: “reconciled, not touching it again”. **The mark is optional:** it doesn't affect the budget, it only helps reconcile the account with the bank. If you've never used it, just skip it — empty circles are fine. **New spending** — three buttons in the bottom right corner.  “+ Transaction” opens an empty form — you fill in the amount, category and account yourself. Above it are two round buttons so you don't have to type. The purple one is the camera: point it at the receipt's QR code, and the app fills in the amount and date by itself (if it knows your country's receipts). The green one is the microphone: say “coffee 6 from account checking”, and the app fills in the amount and account, plus the payee and category if it recognizes them among yours. Either way the same form opens — check it and save. [The article “Transaction form”](entry.md) **Camera and QR icons** — a receipt photo and an e-receipt are attached to the transaction. [What it is](#badges) **PDF icon** — a file is attached to the transaction: a bill, an invoice, an online store receipt. [What it is](#badges) **Fork icon** — the amount is split into parts across different categories. [What it is](#badges) **Hash signs — tags** — your “what for” labels; a transaction can have several. [What it is](#tags) The screen comes in two views Don't worry if your screen doesn't look like the picture above. The buttons in the bottom right corner fold away so they don't cover your transactions.    To bring back the camera and microphone, scroll the feed up a little — the buttons expand again. You can tap “+” in either view: it always opens the new transaction form. Icons and tags in a row Small icons next to a transaction say it has something extra: an attached receipt, a file or several categories. They don't do anything by themselves — to see what's attached, tap the row.  Camera — a receipt photo A picture of a paper receipt, a price tag or anything else you'd like to keep next to the purchase.  **Don't overdo it.** Attach photos to what you'll really need, not to every loaf of bread. [Why](#attach-weight)  The transaction form has a “Photos and PDFs” field. Tap “Add” and choose “Take a photo” or “Pick from the gallery”. You can attach several photos. It comes in handy when a month later you need to return something under warranty or remember what was in that $47.55 purchase. The photo is stored on the phone; for it to appear on your other devices too, turn on “Sync photos” in the sync settings.  QR square — an e-receipt The code or link to the receipt that the register issued.  Many receipts have a QR code printed at the bottom — you can use it to find the receipt in the store's or tax service's system. The transaction form has an “E-receipt (URL or code)” field: paste the link there, or tap the scanner icon and point the camera at the QR code. If the app knows your country's receipts, it also checks the receipt against the form: it fills in the amount if you haven't typed it yet, and if the amounts differ, it tells you and offers to fix it. The scanner doesn't change the date in the form. A receipt from an unfamiliar country is simply saved as is — and still comes in handy: in the transaction card you can copy the code and open the link.  “PDF” sheet — an attached file A bill, a utility invoice, an online store receipt — anything that arrives as a file.  **Don't overdo it.** A PDF isn't compressed when added — the file is stored as is. [Why](#attach-weight)  The same “Photos and PDFs” field in the form: “Add” → “Pick a PDF”. The file sits next to the transaction — no more hunting for the bill in your email or “Downloads”. Tap an attached PDF — “Open” (in a PDF app) and “Save to file” (a copy to a folder you choose) appear at the bottom.  Every photo has weight The database itself doesn't get fat from photos: it stores only a link to the file. But the file lives on the phone and, more importantly, goes in full into **every backup**. By default up to 19 backups are kept — 7 frequent and 12 monthly, on the phone and in the cloud. So a single 300 KB receipt photo can take up almost 6 MB in backups, and a hundred such photos more than half a gigabyte. If “Sync photos” is on, each one also travels to the cloud and to your other devices. Same with PDFs, except they aren't compressed at all when added. **The rule is simple:** attach what you'll need — a warranty card, a receipt for an expensive purchase, a bill for your records. Bread and milk can do without photos. And an e-receipt (QR) weighs as much as a line of text — you can save it for every purchase.  Fork — the amount is split into parts One purchase — several categories. In the form it's “Split the amount” in the category list; in the transaction card the parts sit under the “Split” heading.  At “Target” in the screenshot you paid $86 in one payment, but bought both food and cleaning supplies. If you recorded it all in “Groceries”, the groceries envelope would shrink by an extra $25, while “Household supplies” would stay untouched — and the budget would start lying. So the amount is split: $61 to “Groceries”, $25 to “Household supplies”. In the feed such a transaction has a chip for each part, and its card has a “Split” section. You can split the amount in the transaction form when choosing the category. Cash back at the checkout is a split too You pay $100 by card at the store and ask the cashier for $30 in cash. The bank shows one charge for $100, but really two things happened: $70 went on groceries, and $30 just moved from your card into your wallet.  Record a $100 transaction from the “Checking” account and split the amount. The first part — $70, category “Groceries”. The second part — $30: in the category picker, scroll to the “Transfers” section and choose “Transfer: Cash”. The feed shows a “Transfer: Cash” chip, the “Cash” account goes up by $30, and the groceries envelope shrinks by exactly $70. Record it all in “Groceries”, and the budget will think you ate $30 more, while your wallet shows less than it actually holds.  A line of hash signs — tags Your labels on top of categories: “#cottage”, “#split”, “#vacation”. A transaction can have as many as you like.  A category answers “what did I spend on”, and a tag answers “what for”. Milk and bread at “Whole Foods” are “Groceries”, but they were bought for the cottage. Tag them “#cottage” — and later you'll see at a glance what summer at the cottage cost, even though the money went to groceries, gas and building supplies. “Trader Joe's” in the screenshot has two tags at once: groceries for the cottage, and paid half-and-half with a friend. A transaction can have as many tags as you like. How to add a tag  In the transaction form, under the note, tap the “Tags” field. A list opens, with recent tags at the top. Check the ones you need. The tag you need doesn't exist yet? Type its name in the “Find or create a tag” line and tap “Create tag “…””. Tap “Done”. Where to look later  **How much was spent under a tag** — the “Payees and tags” icon in the header (callout 2), the “Tags” tab. Tap a tag to open its screen: how much went out over all time, by category and by month, and all the transactions. **Find transactions** — type “#” and the start of the tag in the search: “#cott” shows everything for the cottage. **Who owes whom** — for a tag like “#split”, turn on “Settle up” in the “⋮” menu on its screen. The app will show how much more to collect or to return to break even. The tag in the row isn't tappable — it's a label, not a button. There are also: **two arrows** — a transfer between your accounts; **a little calendar with an arrow** — a transaction entered from a scheduled payment; **a sticky note** — a note: an entry without an amount, a reminder to yourself. The “⋮” menu Everything here is about how to show the feed. Not a single item changes or deletes your entries — try them without worry.    Select transactions One action on a dozen rows at once.  Need to put a red flag on a dozen purchases to check them against the statement? You don't need to open each one. Turn on selection and check the rows — their total appears at the bottom (handy for adding up receipts, too). Tap the “⋮” next to the total: you can set a category, a flag or the “cleared” mark for all of them at once, repeat them with today's date, move them to another account, or delete them. The last item, “Clear the selection”, leaves selection without changing anything. The shortcut: press and hold any row.  Filter Keep only what you need in the feed.  For example: “café spending last month, card only”. You can filter by type, period, category, payee, account, amount and tag. Filters add up — each next one narrows the feed. While a filter is on, a number lights up on the “⋮” — a reminder that the feed isn't complete right now. Otherwise it's easy to think transactions have vanished. **Right after installing:** no filters. **Resets by itself:** when you switch budgets — another budget has its own categories and accounts. **See also:** [the reports filter](reports.md).  Sorting How to arrange transactions within one day.  Days always go as in a calendar — the latest at the top, and that can't be changed. But within a day you can set your own order: big spending at the top (“Descending”), small stuff at the top (“Ascending”), or income first. The chosen order is written right in the menu item — so that a week later you aren't surprised why a day looks “shuffled”. **Right after installing:** in the order entered. **Also works:** on the account screen, in a category's transactions and for a payee.  Daily total How much went out in a day — right next to the date.  Turn on “Expenses only” — and to the right of each date you'll see how much you spent that day. A great way to catch the “expensive” days: a Saturday with the market and the movies stands out right away. “Expenses and income” shows the difference as one signed number: “−100” — the day went into the minus, “+1,400” — a paycheck came in. Transfers between your own accounts and starting balances don't count: they're not spending, the money just moved. **Right after installing:** not shown. **Also works:** on the account screen and in a category's transactions.  Hints All of this screen's hints in one place.  In the app, hints appear one at a time — when they're useful, so as not to bury you in everything at once. Here they're all gathered, even the ones you haven't reached yet.  Help Center This article on the website: it opens in your browser, in the app's language. What you can do with a row There are no “edit” and “delete” buttons in the row — so they don't get in the way of reading. Instead, tap the row or swipe it sideways with your finger.   You tapped a transaction — what's inside The transaction card slides up from the bottom: everything you recorded about it, on one sheet. Nothing changes until you tap “Edit” — you can look at it calmly.     **Big at the top** — the signed amount: minus is an expense, plus is income. **Payee, category, account, date** — what you recorded in the form. **Receipt** — the e-receipt. “Copy” puts the code on the clipboard so you can paste it wherever you need. If it's a link, there's also “Open” — the receipt opens in the browser. **Tags** — the transaction's labels as chips, as in the feed: “#cottage”. **Photos** — thumbnails of the attached pictures and PDFs. Tap a picture to open it full screen. **Split parts** — for a split amount: each part with its own category, note and amount. Buttons at the bottom  **“Edit”** — open this transaction in the form and change anything. **“Repeat”** — a new transaction with the same payee, category and amount. Handy for what you buy often: coffee, transit, lunch. **“Create a scheduled payment”** — make a regular payment out of this transaction: rent, a subscription, a loan. All that's left is to choose how often it repeats. A split amount and a transfer have only “Edit”: the app won't repeat them half by half.
reports: Reports Ten reports: where your money goes, how spending changes, where income comes from, and whether your net worth is growing. How the tab works One report on screen at a time. At the top is which report and for what period, below it the report itself. The app remembers the report and the period: open “Spending trend” for six months, and next time that's what opens.    **Report name** — tap it to open the list of all reports (screenshot below). **Filters** — the funnel: period, categories, accounts, tags. The number on it is how many filters are on.  Turn off the “Rent” category — it disappears from the spending reports, and your everyday spending picture gets clearer. Filters are remembered for each budget. **Period** — the “‹ ›” arrows move the window one month back or forward, and tapping the label opens the period picker: a month, 3, 6, 12 months, year to date, or your own range.  Moved away from the current month? “Today” appears next to it, to get back. Each report has its own period: spending is handy to view by month, and the trend by year. **View** — some reports have several views: donut, bubbles, tiles, table or chart. The choice is remembered for each report. **List** — the same numbers as rows: color, name, amount, percent. Tap a row to open the category or payee screen.    Spending Where the money goes and how that changes. Where the money went Spending over the period by category — the main “where did it all go” report. Three views of the same thing: pick whichever is clearer to you.     Donut, bubbles, tiles Switch between them with the icons on the right above the picture. The donut is familiar; bubbles and tiles show small categories better next to big ones.  Tapping Tap a slice of the donut, a bubble or a tile — it's highlighted, and its row lights up in the list. A second tap opens that category's screen.  What's counted Spending minus refunds, without transfers between your own accounts. In the screenshot, $5,893 went out over three months, 61% of it on rent.  Want to see everyday spending without rent and utilities? Remove them in the “Categories” filter. Spending trend Is your spending rising or falling — by month, with the average and a trend line.    At the top Average spending per month and where it's heading: “rising ≈ $38.20/mo” or “falling”.  The chart Bars are each month's spending. The line with dots is the change, the straight line is the trend, the dashed line is the average. The current month is faded: it isn't over yet, so it's left out of the average and the trend.  The “By month” table Each month and how far it is from the average — in dollars and percent. Tap a month on the chart, and the exact amount appears above it. Example: are utilities getting more expensive The overall trend won't tell you: it has all spending at once, and growth in one category gets lost in the rest. Leave just one category in the report.     **“Categories”** — in “Spending trend”, tap the funnel at the top right, then “Categories”: a list of all categories with check boxes opens. **“Deselect all”** — unchecks every category at once instead of one by one. **The category you need** — check “Utilities”. Under “Categories” it now says “1 of 18”. Close the sheet: swipe it down or tap outside it. **The number on the funnel** — how many filters are on. While it's lit, the report doesn't show all spending. Now the report is about utilities alone: $97.27 a month on average, the bills are falling by about $3.87 a month, and October was 20% cheaper than average. The filter is remembered for this report: next time “Spending trend” opens with it. To bring back all categories — “Select all” or “Reset” in the filters sheet. Top payees The same as “Where the money went”, but by payee: who you pay the most.    The same three views Donut, bubbles or tiles — this report keeps its own choice.  Tapping A row or a slice opens the payee screen: all spending with them, by category and by month (article [“Payees and tags”](payees-tags.md)). Deviation Where you're spending more or less than usual this month — at a glance. It compares with your 12 months before the period: the month in progress is compared with the same days of past months, from the 1st to today's date, and a period of several months with a usual month multiplied by their number.    Tiles A tile's size is how much was spent, its color is how much more (reddish) or less (greenish) than usual, in three steps. Gray ones are as usual, within 10%. An outline without fill means the category appeared for the first time.  “Usually” The middle of your past months over the year: one unusually expensive month won't shift it. For the current month — “usually by this date”: November 10 is compared with the same days of past months.  The summary in words Under the tiles — “More than usual”, “Less”, “New” with amounts. “Categories” or “Payees” — chips at the top. Tags How much went under each tag — by month, as a table or a chart.     The table A row per tag, a column per month. “Together” is all tags at once: a transaction with two tags counts in it once. “All spending” is there for comparison.  “Settlements” Tags with “Settle up” turned on, as a separate block: how much to collect or to return.  The chart Up to four tags as lines by month; which ones — you choose above the chart. Money flow Where the money came from, where it went, and how much is left. Money flow The money's whole journey in one picture: from income sources — into the budget — by group — by category.     At the top Income, expenses, “net” (how much is left) and the savings rate — what percent of income wasn't spent.  Ribbons A ribbon's thickness is the amount. Tap a ribbon to see the amount and percent. The green “Remainder” band is money that didn't go anywhere.  How to look at it The picture is wider than the screen: swipe sideways and down. The header with the totals scrolls along with the picture. Income and expenses Month-by-month bookkeeping: how much came in, how much went out by group, what's left.     The table Rows are income by source and expenses by group; a group can be expanded down to categories. At the bottom — each month's “Total” and “Savings rate”.  Tap a number to open the list of transactions it's made of. The table is wider than the screen — swipe sideways.  The chart Each month has two bars: green going up — how much money came in, red going down — how much went out. A thin line shows what's left: above zero, the month ended in the plus; below, you spent more than came in. Above the chart are four numbers for the whole period: income, expenses, total and savings rate. Tap a month, and the numbers show just that month; slide your finger, and they change across the neighboring months; tap the same month again, and it's the whole period again. Age of money How your age of money changed month by month.    The number at the top The age at the end of the period — the same number as on “Overview”.  Why You see whether your buffer is growing. A line going up means you're further and further from “paycheck to paycheck”. What the number means and how it's calculated — in the article [“Overview”](overview.md), section “Age of money in detail”. Net worth Everything you own and everything you owe. Net worth The total of all accounts minus debts — and how it changed.    What's included All accounts in the main currency — both on budget and off budget (savings, deposits), minus credit cards and loans. Accounts in other currencies aren't converted and aren't included in the total.  The table Net worth at the end of each month, with an arrow — up or down. Card debt How much you owe on credit cards — and whether the debt is growing.    The number at the top The debt on all credit cards at the end of the period and how much it grew or shrank over the period.  When you see it The report is in the list only if you have a credit card. How a credit card works in the budget — in the article [“How the budget works”](start.md).
accounts: Accounts Every place your money is kept: cards, your wallet, savings, credit cards. And how much is where right now. Why this screen Here you see where your money is right now: how much is in checking, how much is in your wallet, how much you owe on the credit card. The envelopes on the “Budget” screen answer “for what”, and accounts answer “where”.   Add your accounts Every place money is kept: cards at every bank, your wallet, savings.  Reconcile with the bank Once a week or a month, make sure the app and the bank show the same thing.  Clear out the old Closed a card? Hide it, and the history stays. What's where on the screen Tap any screenshot to open it full screen.    **Section** — a shelf of accounts of one kind. Tap the name to collapse the section.  There are four sections, and which one an account lands in depends on its type. “On budget” is money you divide among envelopes: checking, cash. “Credit cards” — credit cards. “Off budget” — what you're saving or just want to keep in view: savings, a deposit. “Debts” — loans. An empty section isn't shown. More in the section [“On budget or off budget”](#kinds). **Section total** — how much is in all the accounts of the section.  “On budget” in the screenshot is $4,712.98: that's checking and cash together, exactly the money you divide among envelopes on the “Budget” screen. “Credit cards” has a red total — that's debt. **Account** — one row is one wallet, card or deposit. The icon and color come from the account type.  Tap the row to open the account screen: all its transactions, like in “Activity”, but only for this account. Press and hold to open the account menu ([below](#hold)). Swipe left or right — “Edit” or “Delete”. **Balance** — how much is in the account right now according to your records.  This is the sum of all the account's transactions with the starting balance. If it doesn't match the bank, a transaction was forgotten or recorded twice. How to find it — [“Balance reconciliation”](#reconcile). **“Uncleared”** — the total of transactions the bank hasn't processed yet.  Checking in the screenshot shows −$47.55: you've already recorded the purchase at “Whole Foods”, but it's not at the bank yet. When it shows up in your statement, check it off with the circle in the feed (in “Activity” — callout 9), and the line disappears. While there are such transactions, the balance in the app and the balance in your bank's app legitimately differ — by exactly that amount. The mark is optional. If you don't use it, all the account's transactions end up here — that's not an error, the line just doesn't tell you anything then. **“Credit cards”** — a separate section for credit cards. The red total is how much you owe the bank. For each credit card the app creates a special category on the “Budget” screen by itself — leave it alone.  Credit card spending shrinks envelopes just like debit card spending. But the app sets aside the money for paying it off by itself — into the “Card payments” group on the “Budget” screen. A credit card payment is a transfer from your debit card to the credit card. **The special category.** When you create an account of the “Credit card” type, the app creates a category with the same name as the card in the “Card payments” group on the “Budget” screen. Under its name it says “Card debt …”. The app sets money aside in it for the payment: spent $35 on the credit card — $35 moved here from the purchase's envelope. **Leave this category alone** — and the app won't let you touch it anyway: it can't be renamed, deleted or moved to another group, and you can't add your own category to the “Card payments” group. The app uses it to count the debt of this particular card. Rename the card on the “Accounts” screen — the category renames itself. Change the card to another type — the category disappears, and its money goes back to “unassigned”. One thing with it is still yours: **the debt the card had before you started tracking**. The app doesn't set money aside for it — to pay it off, you put money into this category like any envelope, a little at a time or all at once. **“Off budget”** — accounts whose money isn't divided among envelopes: savings, a deposit. How they differ — [below](#kinds). **The “⋮” menu** — add an account and set up how the list looks. Explained [below](#menu). On budget or off budget The main question about each account: do you divide its money among envelopes? The answer decides where the account appears on this screen and whether its money reaches the “Budget” screen.   On budget Checking, cash, a credit card — what you spend from every day. Every dollar here should be in some envelope. A paycheck lands in checking — it goes to “unassigned”.  Off budget Savings, a deposit, investments, a loan — what you want to see but don't spend every day. This money has no envelopes. Moved money from savings to checking? It shows up in “unassigned”, and you can hand it out. A new account lands in its section by itself, by type: “Cash” and “Bank account” go to “On budget”, “Credit card” to “Credit cards”, “Loan” to “Debts”, “Tracking” to “Off budget”. Loans and “Tracking” accounts have no envelopes. The “⋮” menu A new account and how to show the list.    Add an account A new card, wallet or deposit.   Tap “Add an account”. Choose a type: “Cash”, “Bank account”, “Credit card”, “Loan” or “Tracking”. The type decides the section and the icon. Enter a name — whatever you call this account: “Chase card”, “Wallet”. Enter how much is in the account today — the amount from your bank's app or your wallet. Save. The amount becomes the starting balance. For cash and a bank account it goes straight to “unassigned” on the “Budget” screen — hand it out to the envelopes.  Running balances Show the balance after each transaction — for all accounts at once.  The same as “Running balance” in a single account's menu, only for all of them. **Right after installing:** off.  Hidden accounts Show hidden accounts at the bottom of the list.  The number in parentheses is how many there are. While there are no hidden accounts, the item is gray, as in the screenshot. Each hidden account in the list has a “Restore” button.  Hints All of this screen's hints in one place.  Help Center This article on the website: it opens in your browser, in the app's language. What you can do with a row An account row has no buttons. Tap it, press and hold, or swipe it sideways.   The account menu — press and hold An account row has no “⋮” of its own, so as not to take space from the name. The menu opens with a long press right where your finger is. The same items are in the “⋮” on the account's own screen.    Balance reconciliation Check that the app and the bank show the same thing.   Open your bank's app and see how much is in the account. In “Accounts”, press and hold this account and choose “Balance reconciliation”. The dialog says “In the app: …”. Below, in the “Actual balance at the bank” field, enter the amount from the bank and tap “Reconcile”. It matches — the app says “Balance reconciled ✓”. All of the account's transactions up to today get a lock, and “Reconciled” with the date appears under the account. It doesn't match — the “The balance does not match” dialog shows the difference. First look for a forgotten or extra transaction. Can't find one? Tap “Create an adjustment”: the app adds a transaction for that difference, and you fill in the category, payee and note yourself. Transactions with a lock count as checked: editing one asks for confirmation, so that what's reconciled doesn't drift by accident.  Running balance Show under each of this account's transactions how much the account held after it.  Handy for finding where the balance parted ways with the bank statement: go through the transactions and compare balances row by row. It turns on only for this account; for all at once — “Running balances” in the “⋮” menu.  Hide the account Remove an account you no longer use from the list.  Closed a card? You can't delete it — it has history. A hidden account disappears from the list, but its transactions stay in the history and reports. To bring it back: “⋮” → “Hidden accounts” — they appear at the bottom of the list with a “Restore” button.  Edit the account Change the account's name, type, icon and color, and for an account in another currency — the currency.  The same sheet opens when you swipe the row left. If the account has a starting balance, the sheet has a “Starting balance” row with the date and amount — tap it to open that transaction itself, and fix it like any other.  Delete the account Only an account without a single transaction.  If the account already has transactions, the app says how many and offers to hide the account instead of deleting it — reports and balances need the history. The same with a swipe to the right.
entry: Transaction form How to record a purchase, income, a transfer or a purchase split across several categories — and what each field does. Why this screen This is where you record everything that happens to your money: a purchase, a paycheck, a transfer from one card to another. The faster you record, the more honest the budget — so the essentials of the form can be done right at the checkout, in a few taps.   Open it “+ Transaction” on any tab. From an account or category screen, the form opens with them already filled in. Even faster — a widget on the home screen.  The minimum Amount, category and account. The payee, note and everything else are optional.  Not only by hand The camera above the “+” reads the receipt's QR code, the microphone a phrase like “coffee 6 Fun & hobbies”. Both buttons open this same form, already filled in. What's where on the screen This is how the form looks right after you tap “+”. The amount keypad opens right away: you almost always start with the amount. Tap any screenshot to open it full screen.    **Close** — the cross. If something is already typed, the app asks “Leave without saving?” — “Stay” or “Don't save”. **“Outgoing” / “Incoming”** — an expense or income. The choice decides the amount's sign and the header color: reddish — an expense, green — income, gray — a transfer.  Choose “Incoming” and a payee — the app puts this month's income category in by itself: that way a paycheck goes straight into “unassigned” on the “Budget” screen. Tap the “Category” field for income — the “Where to put the income” sheet opens: “Income for November”, “Income for December” or “To an expense category…” (a refund, your share of a shared purchase). A paycheck is recorded for next month once your age of money reaches 30 days — why and what changes is covered in the article [“Overview”](overview.md), section “Age of money in detail”. **Amount** — typed on the keypad below. If the keypad is hidden, tap the amount to bring it back. **Payee** — who you paid or who the money came from: “Whole Foods”, “Employer”. Transfers between your own accounts are here too.  Choose a payee you've recorded before — the app fills in the category and note like last time. It fills only empty fields: if you've already chosen a category, it stays. A new payee is created from the search: type the name and choose “Create “…””. To remove the payee from a transaction, use the cross on the right of the field. More — [below](#pickers). **Category** — the envelope the money left. Without it, a purchase won't reduce any row on the “Budget” screen. **Account** — where the money left from or arrived to: checking, wallet, credit card. The icon and color are the same as in the account list. **Date** — today, if you don't touch it. Tap it to open a calendar.  A date more than a month ahead — the app asks again: “The transaction will be recorded on …, more than a month ahead. Record it?”. That catches a typo in the year. **Amount keypad** — the app's own, with a calculator. Explained [below](#keypad). The amount keypad The phone's regular keyboard is awkward for amounts: small digits, no operations, the decimal point somewhere on a second screen. The form has its own — big and with a calculator.  It does the math A receipt for two, two purchases on one card — calculate right in the field.  Type 120, tap “+”, type 35 and tap “=” — the amount becomes 155. “+”, “−”, “×” and “÷” all work. The chosen operation stays highlighted while you type the second number.  Decimal point or cents How to type the fractional part is up to you.  **With a decimal point** — like a calculator: 12, point, 50 is 12.50. While you're typing the cents, the decimal point key is highlighted. **From cents** — like a card terminal: 1250 is 12.50. Instead of a decimal point the keypad has a “00” key: “3”, “00”, “00” is 300.00. Switch it in “Settings → Language and formats → Amount entry”. **Right after installing:** with a decimal point.  Erase Tap to erase the last digit. Press and hold to erase everything at once, together with an operation you've started.  “Done” Hides the keypad, revealing the other fields and the “Save” button underneath. The system Back button does the same.  Which hand The digits under your thumb.  “For the right hand” — digits on the right, operations and “Done” on the left (as in the screenshot). “For the left hand” — the other way round. “Settings → Language and formats → Amount keypad”. **Right after installing:** for the right hand. Choosing the payee and category Both fields open a list from the bottom of the screen. At the top — search: type a couple of letters, and the list narrows.     Transfers — in the payee list The money went to your own account? Choose it in the “Transfers” section: “Transfer: Visa”.  Under the account name is its balance, so you don't pick the wrong one. Off-budget accounts (savings, a deposit) are in their own section below. How a transfer works — [below](#transfer).  New payee Not in the list? Type the name in the search and choose “Create “…””.  You don't need to set up payees in advance: the list builds up by itself as you record. To rename or delete — “Settings → Payees”.  “Frequently used” Chips with the categories you choose most often. One tap and you're done.  Search also understands the group name. Can't find it? Choose “Create “…” in group”: the new category appears right away on the “Budget” screen too.  “Split the amount” One purchase — several categories. Explained [below](#split). A filled-in transaction The purchase at “Whole Foods” from the “Activity” article: with a tag, an e-receipt and a photo. The keypad is hidden and “Additional” is expanded — all of the form's fields are visible.    **Note** — what you bought or why: “Milk, eggs, bread”. It shows in the feed in italics and can be found with search.  The amount is optional: an entry without an amount is a note about an event. For example: oil changed at 85,000 km, gave Andrew the keys to the cottage. It still needs an account and a category.
