On the first tap of “Save” the app answers “Enter an amount”, on the second “Enter an amount. Tap again and it will be saved without one”, and the third tap saves the entry. Later, search in “Activity” finds it: search looks at note text too — type oil, for example. **“Additional”** — the rarely used fields in one card. Tap the header to collapse or expand the card.  A collapsed card is one line, with icons on the right for the fields hidden in it: tag, receipt, photo, “Cleared”, flag. A filled-in field is always visible, even in a collapsed card. The app remembers your choice. **Right after installing:** collapsed. **Tags** — labels on top of the category: “#cottage”, “#vacation”. The picker sheet — [below](#tags). **E-receipt** — the code or link from the receipt. The scanner icon on the right points the camera at a QR code, “+” adds another receipt.  If the app knows your country's receipts, it checks the receipt against the form: it fills in the amount if there isn't one yet, and if the amounts differ, it shows a line under the field and offers “Fix”. A receipt never changes the date. More about receipts and photos — in the article [“Activity”](transactions.md). **Photos and PDFs** — “Add” — take a picture of a receipt, pick a photo from the gallery or a PDF. The cross on a thumbnail removes it.  Don't overdo it: every photo goes into all backups and, if it's on, into the cloud. More — in the article [“Activity”](transactions.md). **“Cleared”** — check it when the transaction shows up on your bank statement. The circle in the feed row does the same.  The mark is optional: it doesn't affect the budget, it only helps reconcile the account with the bank. If you've never used it, just skip it — empty circles are fine. **Flag** — a colored “come back later” mark: to check, to wait for a refund, to discuss. A little flag appears in the feed row. **Delete the transaction** — only for a transaction that's already recorded. The app asks again. **“Save”** — record it. Without an account or a category the app won't save and tells you what to choose. A zero amount is allowed: such an entry becomes a reminder note in the feed. A transfer between your own accounts Withdrew cash, paid off a credit card, moved money to a deposit — that's not spending, it's money moving. Record such transactions as transfers, otherwise the budget will count them as expenses.     Where to — in the “Payee” field Choose an account in the “Transfers” section. The form's header turns gray.  The screenshot shows a credit card payment: $300 from “Checking” to “Visa”. Two rows appear in the feed: a minus on checking and a plus on the credit card.  “No category needed” The money is still yours — it just moved. The envelopes on the “Budget” screen don't change.  The exception is a transfer between a budget account and an off-budget one (to savings, for example). Then money leaves the envelopes or enters them, and the app asks for a category.  “Outgoing” and “Incoming” for a transfer The direction is from the point of view of the account in the “Account” field.  **“Outgoing”** — money leaves this account for the account in the “Payee” field. A red circle glows softly behind the amount. **“Incoming”** — money arrives on this account from the one in “Payee”. The circle is green. A transfer's header is gray either way.  One transfer — two ways to record it A $300 payment from “Checking” to “Visa” can be recorded from either side. The result is the same.   **Leaving checking** (left screenshot): “Account” — Checking, “Payee” — “Transfer: Visa”, “Outgoing”, red glow. **Arriving on the credit card** (right screenshot): “Account” — Visa, “Payee” — “Transfer: Checking”, “Incoming”, green glow. Either way the same two rows appear in the feed: −300 on Checking and +300 on Visa, both with the transfer icon. Choose whichever is handier: reconciling the checking statement — record it as leaving checking; your bank's app says “credit card payment received” — record it as arriving on the card. From an account screen, the form opens with that account by itself. **Record a transfer once.** The app adds the other side by itself. Record it leaving checking and then also arriving on the credit card, and the transfer doubles: $600 leaves checking, and $600 arrives on the card instead of $300.  Different currencies From a dollar card to a euro account — the form offers conversion by itself.  Under the payee, fields appear: “Credited” — how much arrives on the second account — and “Rate”, with a button that flips the rate's direction. Change the amount, and “Credited” is recalculated; change the rate — the same; enter “Credited” — and the rate is recalculated. A split amount One purchase — several envelopes: at “Target” you bought food for $61 and cleaning supplies for $25. Record it as one transaction, but in two categories — then both envelopes shrink honestly.    “Split” Appears instead of the “Category” field when you choose “Split the amount”. Next to it — the “Total” of the parts.  A part Its own category, amount and note. Tap the category or amount — only this part changes.  A part can be a transfer too: asked for cash back at the checkout — $70 to “Groceries” and $30 as “Transfer: Cash”. An example with numbers — in the article [“Activity”](transactions.md).  “+ tag” A tag just for this part. A tag from the form's “Tags” field applies to the whole purchase at once.  “Add a part” One more line. The cross to the right of an extra part removes it.  “Cancel” Go back to one category for the whole amount. The parts don't add up to the total? Explained [below](#split-mismatch). The parts don't add up to the amount Made a mistake in one part? The app won't fix it silently — it shows the difference right under the parts and offers a way to close it.     “Split parts exceed the total by …” / “… left to split” How far the parts are from the total. The line appears under the parts by itself while you edit.  While you're editing, the line is yellow — it's a hint. Tap “Save” with amounts that don't add up, and the line turns red, and the form won't save the transaction until the amounts match. The same fix button is also in the message at the bottom of the screen.  “Increase to …” / “Reduce to …” One tap — and the total becomes equal to the sum of the parts.  On the left: in the second part you typed 35 instead of 25. Together the parts make $96, while the total is $86: “Split parts exceed the total by $10.00”, and the “Increase to $96.00” button adds those 10 to the total. On the right it's the other way round: 15 instead of 25 — “$10.00 left to split”, and the “Reduce to $76.00” button takes 10 away. **The button fixes the total, not the part.** If the total is right — as on the receipt — and you made the mistake in a part, fix the part itself: tap its amount and type the right one. Refund for a returned item Returned spoiled milk, took back a jacket that didn't fit — the money came back. That's not income: record it as a refund to the same category you paid from.     How to record it A refund is money that came from the store back to the category it left from.   “+ Transaction” → “Incoming”. The refund amount. Payee — the same store. Account — where the money was returned, usually the same card. Out of habit, the app puts “Income for November” in “Category” (left screenshot). Tap the “Category” field → “To an expense category…” → choose the category you bought from: “Groceries”. Note — optional: “Refund: spoiled milk”. Save.  What changes The “Groceries” envelope is topped up, “unassigned” isn't.   On the “Budget” screen, “Groceries” shows “spent” $3 lower, and the balance grows by the same amount. “Unassigned” doesn't change: you didn't earn it, you got your own money back. On the category and store screens, spending is counted after refunds. In the “Overview” calendar, a day with only refunds is marked with an empty ring. Refunded to a credit card? The card's debt goes down, and with it the amount set aside for paying it in “Card payments”.  What if you record it as income The budget will lie twice.  “Income for November” adds $3 to “unassigned” as if you'd earned it, while “Groceries” keeps a purchase that didn't really happen. The “Income and expenses” report shows both income and expenses higher than they really are.  Why not delete the purchase You can delete it if you returned everything the same day.  If the purchase has already cleared the bank or been reconciled, or you returned only part of it, record the refund as a separate transaction. The bank statement will have two lines, the purchase and the refund — let the app have two as well: the reconciliation will match. Money a friend paid you back for their half of a shared purchase is recorded the same way: “Incoming”, from the friend, to the purchase's category. Tags The “Tags” field in “Additional” opens a picker sheet.    Check the tags you need — recent ones are at the top, with the number of transactions on the right. The one you need isn't there? Type its name in the “Find or create a tag” line and choose “Create tag “…””. Tap “Done”. The selection isn't lost even if you swipe the sheet down. Why tags are useful and where to see the totals later — in the article [“Activity”](transactions.md). No time? — “To inbox” At the checkout you sometimes have only a second: you remember the amount, but there's no time to pick a category and account.  Turn on “Settings → Data → Inbox”. Now, if the form has an amount but no category or account, the button says **“To inbox”** instead of “Save”, and on the amount keypad it saves right away. The transaction is recorded, but marked “Sort”. While there are such transactions, a strip hangs above the navigation, and there's a notice on “Overview”. Tap it — the form opens them one by one, in the order you recorded them: handy for remembering the day store by store. **Right after installing:** off. It's especially handy with voice: say the purchase at the checkout — and sort out at home whatever voice didn't recognize. The scenario — in the article [“Voice input”](voice.md#inbox). What you can do in the form A short cheat sheet of gestures and buttons.
voice: Voice input Say the purchase in one phrase — “Whole Foods 70 Groceries” — and the app opens the form already filled in. Check it and save. Why At the checkout your hands are full, but you need to record the purchase right away, while you remember. Typing the amount, choosing the payee, category and account — that's five taps. By voice — one phrase. Voice doesn't record anything by itself. It fills in the transaction form, and you're the one who saves it — so a recognition mistake never slips into the budget unnoticed. The microphone button is green, above “+ Transaction” on “Overview”, in “Activity”, and on the account and category screens. The first time    **What to say** — the amount and your own names: category, store, account. **Example** — a phrase from your own budget: your most frequent category and a typical amount. Repeat it — and it will work. **Where it goes** — into the transaction form, where you can check and fix everything. **“Speak”** — turns on the microphone. The first time, the sheet doesn't turn it on by itself: read what to say first. After that, the microphone turns on as soon as you open the sheet. The app asks for microphone permission — allow it. Speak, then tap “Done” or just stop talking: the recognized phrase appears on the sheet, and the form opens. What to say Start with the amount and category, then add the rest. The example under the microphone grows with you: two successful phrases in a row — and it shows the next step. The steps on the demo budget:      The screenshot shows the form after the phrase “Whole Foods 70 Groceries from account Checking”. The date is today. Check it and tap “Done”, then “Save”.  Words the app understands  **“transfer”** — a transfer between accounts; **“income”** — money came in. Without these words, the phrase is an expense. **“from account …”** or **“from …”** — which account it's from; **“to account …”** or **“to …”** — which account it goes to. You can leave out the word “account”. **“note”** — everything after this word becomes the note. So say it last. **“category …”** — if a category name sounds like a store name and the app mixes them up.  Amount In digits or words — recognition turns “two hundred fifty” into 250 by itself. Cents go after a decimal point: “25.50”. If the phrase has several numbers, the amount is the first one. How names are recognized The app looks for **your** names in the phrase: payees, categories and accounts from this budget. It doesn't create new ones — name a store that isn't in the budget yet, and the “Payee” field stays empty.  The payee brings the category with it Once the payee is recognized, the category and note fill in from its past transactions, as if you'd picked it in the form by hand. Saying “Whole Foods 70” is enough — the “Groceries” category fills in by itself.  How many words are needed For a payee, one word from the name is enough. A category with several words needs at least two of them — so that “Health & medical” isn't confused with “Health”. A name said in full is always recognized.  An example with made-up names (“Chase 100 groceries Home Depot”) would teach a phrase that doesn't exist in your budget: repeat it, and you'd get an empty form. So the example is always built from your own data — your most frequent purchase, your accounts, a recent note. Didn't get it all — “To inbox” Voice recognized the amount, but not the category or store. No time to sort it out at the checkout, and you don't want to lose the purchase. That's what the “Inbox” is for.  Record it now, sort it out at home  Turn on “Settings → Data → Inbox” once. At the checkout, say the phrase as usual. At the end, add “note” and a couple of words about the purchase — for example, “note pharmacy near home”. The note is saved even if the store and category weren't recognized. Something's missing in the form? Instead of “Save” there's a “To inbox” button, and on the amount keypad too. Tap it — the purchase is recorded and marked “Sort”. At home, tap the strip above the navigation or the notice on “Overview”. The form opens these purchases one by one, in the order you recorded them: “Inbox · 1 of 3”. Choose a category and account — “Save”. The amount, date and everything voice managed to recognize are already in the transaction — with them and the note, it's easy to remember the purchase. If the account was recognized, the purchase has already reduced its balance, and on “Budget” it sits in the “No category” row until you sort it. If the account wasn't recognized, the purchase waits outside the budget and enters it once you choose the account.  A transfer between accounts and a split amount: they need both accounts or all the parts at once. It won't go without an amount either: if voice didn't catch the number, type it in the form. More about the “Inbox” in the article [“Transaction form”](entry.md#inbox). If it didn't understand   If nothing was recognized, the example on the sheet becomes one step simpler. If a name was recognized but not the amount, the example stays the same: most likely the phrase just got cut off. Language The app listens in the interface language — the one chosen in “Settings”, “Appearance” section → “Language and formats” → “Interface language”. More in the article [“Settings”](settings.md#formats). Under the example it says which language it's listening in.  “The interface language is not installed for speech recognition — listening in …” The phone has no recognition model for this language, so the app listens in the phone's language. Add the language in the phone's speech recognition settings — and the line goes away.  The words “transfer”, “income”, “note” — in your language Each language has its own keywords: in Ukrainian “переказ”, “дохід”, “нотатка”, in Russian “перевод”, “доход”, “заметка”. The example under the microphone always shows the words of your language.
receipt: Receipt scanner Point the camera at the receipt's QR code — the app fills in the amount and date, and recognizes a store you've seen before by its register number, filling in the payee, category and account. Why Receipts pile up in your pocket, and in the evening you have to remember where, how much and when. The scanner takes the amount and date from the receipt — no typos in the numbers, and the real day of the purchase, even if you enter the receipt the next day. The receipt is saved in the transaction as an e-receipt: you can throw away the paper one. Where the button is The purple button with a QR code sits above “+ Transaction” on “Overview”, in “Activity”, and on the account and category screens. It shows only if the app knows your country's receipts:    A language says nothing about the country you shop in: people write in Russian both in Ukraine and in Kazakhstan, and the receipts there are different. The currency, on the other hand, you chose yourself — and it tells where you pay. In other countries there's no button. But you can save the code from any receipt in a transaction — with the scanner icon in the form's “E-receipt” field ([below](#form)). And to teach the app to read your country's receipts, send us a few — [how](#your-country). How to scan     Tap the purple button. The first three times, the app explains how it learns from receipts (screenshot). Tap “Scan”. Once it has recognized a store, it won't explain again. The camera opens: “Point the camera at the QR code on the receipt”. The code is read by itself, you don't need to tap anything. The transaction form opens with the amount, date and receipt. Check it and tap “Save”. Is the receipt a photo or a PDF on your phone? Under the camera — “Pick from the gallery” and “Pick a PDF”. What comes from the receipt A receipt's QR code holds no store name and no list of purchases — only the amount, the date and time, the receipt number and the register number. So:    A register always belongs to one store. At a supermarket you end up in one line or another — with Ukrainian receipts the app also recognizes a neighboring register of the same store. If neighboring registers lead to different payees, the app stays quiet: better to pick the store yourself than to get the wrong one. A new store For the first receipt from a new store, the app fills in only the amount and date — and opens the payee picker right away.      Find the store in the list or type a new name. The category fills in by itself if you've bought from this payee before. Choose the account: you haven't paid at this store yet, so the app doesn't know it. “Save”. The next receipt from this register arrives with the payee, category and account already filled in. Repeats and errors   Some register services print a link to their own website on the receipt, with no amount or date — the app can't read such a receipt. A receipt from a file: “Share” The receipt came by email, Viber or in your bank's app as an image or a PDF? Tap “Share” there and choose “My Budget”.   A familiar receipt is found — the form opens as it does after the camera, and the app asks “Attach the file to the transaction?”. The e-receipt is added either way; attach the file if you want to see the receipt itself. There's no receipt in the file, or it's an unfamiliar one — the app says why and offers “Fill in manually”: the form opens with the file already attached. A receipt in the form In the transaction form, under “Additional”, there's an “E-receipt” field with a scanner icon. It works with **any** QR code, in any country: it puts whatever the code says into the field. If the receipt is a familiar one, the app checks it against the form: it fills in the amount if there isn't one yet, and if the amounts differ, it shows the line “The receipt has a different amount: …” and offers “Fix”. A receipt doesn't change the date in an open form. More in the article [“Transaction form”](entry.md). A saved receipt shows as an icon in the transaction row, and in the transaction card as “Copy” and “Open” buttons. More in the article [“Activity”](transactions.md). Teach the app your country's receipts The app reads a receipt without the internet: everything it needs — the amount and date — has to be in the QR code itself. In many countries that's the case: a fiscal receipt's QR code holds the amount, date and register number. If that's true in your country too, we can add its receipts.  Send 5–10 receipts  Take receipts from different stores: a supermarket chain, a pharmacy, a gas station, a small shop. E-receipts — a PDF or an image from an email — work too. Photograph each so that the QR code and the total are clearly visible. Send them to “Telegram chat” or by email with “Suggest an improvement” — both in “Settings”, “Help & contact” section. Mention your country. Several receipts are needed to make sure the code is built the same way across different registers and chains. One receipt can't tell you that.  We need only the QR code, the amount and the date. The last digits of your card, the cashier's name, a loyalty card and anything else personal can be covered with a finger or blacked out — it doesn't affect recognition.  If the receipt's QR code holds only a link to a website — no amount and no date — the data is on that website. The app doesn't go there: it promises to work without a server and without registration. Such receipts stay without the scanner, but you can always save their code in the “E-receipt” field.
widgets: Widgets and shortcuts Buttons for recording a purchase right on your phone's home screen: voice, a new transaction, the receipt scanner. One tap and you're in the form — without opening the app or scrolling to the “+”. Why Purchases get recorded while you remember them: at the checkout, on your way out of the store. Every extra tap is an excuse to put it off “until tonight” and forget. A widget on the home screen opens what you need right away: voice, the form, or the camera for a receipt. Five widgets   The colors match the buttons in the app: green for voice, purple for receipts.  The receipt button isn't for everyone Everyone gets the separate “Receipt” widget. But in the three-button widgets, the receipt button shows only if the app knows your country's receipts — by the same rule as the button in the app. The rule is in the article [“Receipt scanner”](receipt.md#where). Otherwise the widget has two buttons. How to add a widget   Press and hold an empty spot on the home screen. Choose “Widgets”. Find “My Budget” and the widget you want. Drag it onto the home screen. The menu names depend on the phone: some have “Widgets” in the home screen menu, others in a separate list. The “Voice”, “Transaction” and “Receipt” widgets take up one cell, like an app icon. Shortcuts A shortcut is the same action as a regular icon: the launcher draws it like app icons, and it lines up with them on any phone.   Press and hold the “My Budget” icon. “Voice” and “Transaction” appear — tap one to open it right away. Or drag a shortcut onto the home screen — it stays there as an icon. There's no shortcut for receipts: a shortcut can't be hidden where the app doesn't know the country's receipts. For receipts, use the “Receipt” widget. What opens   After saving, you stay on “Overview” and see the purchase has made it into the budget.  If a PIN is set The app first asks for your PIN or fingerprint, and right after that opens what you tapped. You don't need to tap anything again.
payees-tags: Payees and tags Who you pay and what for — two slices of your transaction feed, alongside categories. Why this screen Categories answer “where did the money go”. Here are two other slices of the same transaction feed: **who** you pay and **what for**. How much went to “Whole Foods” this year, what the cottage cost, who owes whom for a shared purchase.   How to get there The “Payees and tags” icon in the “Activity” header. Or “Settings → Data → Payees” and “Tags”. Or “All tags ›” in the “My tags” block on “Overview”.  No need to set them up in advance Payees and tags appear by themselves the first time you type them in the transaction form. Here you view, rename and clean them up.  Two tabs “Payees” and “Tags”. The screen remembers which tab you left on. The “Payees” tab Everyone you've paid or received money from. Tap any screenshot to open it full screen.    **Tabs** — “Payees” and “Tags”. **The “⋮” menu** — the order of the payee list and the period of the total. Explained to the right of the second screenshot. **Search** — type a couple of letters of the name. **Payee** — a letter, the name, on the right the total for the period, under the name how many transactions there were in the same period and when the last one was.  The total is “net” and signed: for a store, a minus after refunds; for an employer, a plus. In the screenshot, “Whole Foods” cost $1,111.89 since the start of the year, and “Employer” brought in $16,800. These numbers have no color on purpose: the sign shows the direction. Tap a row — the payee screen opens ([below](#payee)). Swipe left — “Edit”: rename. Swipe right — “Delete”: the app asks again and says how many transactions the payee has. The transactions themselves won't disappear; they'll just be left without a payee. **“Total, this year”** — the label above the list: which period the numbers on the right cover. Choose the period in the “⋮” menu. **“+ New payee”** — add a payee by hand. Usually not needed: the transaction form creates one by itself. List order    Most used Those with the most transactions at the top. This is the setting right after installing.  Recent Those with the most recent transaction at the top.  Alphabetical Handy when you have hundreds of payees.  By amount The biggest at the top: both who you pay the most and who you get the most from. The sign doesn't matter, only the size.  Period “Total, this year” (the default right after installing), “Total, last 12 months” or “Total, all time”. The period sets the amount in each row, “Transactions: N” and the “Most used” and “By amount” orders; the date of the last transaction is always all-time. The year starts on January 1: on January 1 the total starts from zero. The payee screen Everything about one payee: how much, on what and when. “⋮” renames, and the “+” at the bottom starts a new transaction with this payee already filled in.    Period It starts on the current month. The arrows flip through months, and tapping the name opens the “Period” sheet: the same one as in “Reports”.  Want to see everything that went to a payee in a year? Choose a year or your own range, and the screen shows it in full: the total, the categories and all transactions.  “Spending trends” How much was spent with the payee over the period and how much on average per month.  Spending is counted after refunds. If the payee mostly pays you (an employer, a tenant), the block is called “Income trends” and counts income.  “By category” What the money to this payee went toward. Shows up when there are two or more categories.  In the screenshot, Netflix has two categories: home internet in “Phone & internet” and the subscription in “Subscriptions”.  Transactions All transactions with this payee over the period, by day. The “Tags” tab Labels on top of categories: “#cottage”, “#vacation”, “#split”. How to put a tag on a transaction — in the article [“Activity”](transactions.md).    **Tag** — the name, the total over the tag's whole span, the span itself and the number of transactions. For a tag with “Settle up”, the right side shows how much to collect or to return.  The order is: tags with an open settlement first, then by how recent the last transaction is, and tags without transactions at the end. Hidden tags are gathered in a separate “Hidden tags” block at the bottom. Tap — the tag screen ([below](#tag)). Press and hold — a menu: “Rename”, “Settle up”, “Hide from picker”. Swipe left to rename, right to delete. **“+ New tag”** — add a tag by hand. Usually tags are created right in the transaction form. The tag screen Everything that went under one tag — how much, on what and when. This is also where “Settle up” is set up.    Span and transactions The first and last day with transactions under the tag, and how many there are. The screen's totals cover the tag's whole span.  Settle up If “Settle up” is on for the tag: how much is left to break even, and a “N % settled” bar.  Settling up answers “who owes whom” for a shared cost. The app calculates: spent minus received over the tag's whole span.  **“To collect”** — you spent more than you collected. In the screenshot: an $86 purchase at “Target” was split with Andrew, he paid back $43 — $43 is left, 50% settled. **“To return”** — you collected more than you spent: for example, everyone chipped in for a gift, and there's change left over. **“Settled”** in green — everything adds up. Record money from a friend as a refund to the purchase's category, with the same tag — as in the article [“Transaction form”](entry.md), section “Refund for a returned item”. “Settle up” doesn't touch the budget or the reports: it's a helper for you.  “Spent” and “Received” How much went out and came in under the tag. Transfers between your own accounts aren't included.  “By category” What the money under this tag went toward. A tag on one part of a split amount counts only that part.  Transactions All transactions with the tag, by day. The tag's “⋮” menu    Rename The new name appears on all transactions with the tag. The app won't accept a name that's already taken.  Show in “My tags” Add the tag to the “My tags” block on “Overview”. There are four spots; when they're full, the item is gray and says why: “My tags already has 4”.  Settle up Turn the “who owes whom” calculation on or off for this tag.  Hide from picker The tag disappears from the picker sheet in the form, but stays on the transactions. Handy for a vacation that's over. For a hidden tag, this spot says “Show in picker”.  Hints This screen's hints.  Help Center This article on the website: it opens in your browser, in the app's language.  Delete The tag is removed from all transactions; the transactions themselves stay. The app asks again. scheduled: Scheduled payments Rent, subscriptions, your paycheck — everything that repeats. The app remembers due dates, reminds you of them and fills in the amount and category itself. Money in the budget moves only when you confirm the payment. Why this screen Half of a month's spending is known in advance: rent on the 1st, internet on the 5th, a subscription on the 11th, a paycheck twice a month. A scheduled payment is such a transaction, written down once, ahead of time.   Don't forget The app reminds you of the due date with a notification — on the day of the payment or in advance, as you set it up.  Don't type it by hand The due date has come — tap “Confirm”, and the transaction records itself: amount, payee, category, account.  See what's ahead Upcoming payments are on “Overview” in the “What’s ahead” block and in the “Calendar”. You see what money is already promised to. A scheduled payment isn't spending yet. Until you confirm it, account and envelope balances don't change: it only reminds and suggests. What's where on the screen All scheduled payments in one list, the nearest due date at the top. Tap any screenshot to open it full screen.    **Row** — one repeating payment. It's laid out like a transaction row: who and how much, category and account, how it repeats and when it's next due.  The first line is the payee and the signed amount: “−” means money will leave, “+” means it will arrive. The second is the category and account. The third is the frequency and the nearest due date. A payment without a payee shows a dash “———” instead of a name, and the note sits on a fourth line — in the screenshot, “Car insurance”. The list is sorted by the nearest due date. Payments whose due date has already passed are here too, at the top: they're waiting for confirmation — more on that [below](#due). **Frequency and date** — on the left how it repeats, on the right the next due date. After each due date is entered or skipped, the date moves on to the next one by itself. **Flag** — the same colored marker as on a transaction. When the payment is entered, the flag passes to the transaction. **“+ Payment”** — a new scheduled payment. The steps are [below](#new). While there are no scheduled payments, the screen is empty: “No scheduled payments” and the hint “Rent, subscriptions, salary — add one with the Payment button”. A new scheduled payment The form is the same as for a regular transaction, just with a “Repeat” field. Tapping a row in the list opens it too: then it's called “Scheduled payment” and edits the existing one.     **Amount** — type it on the app's keypad and tap “Done”. Above the amount — “− Outgoing” for a payment and “+ Incoming” for a paycheck. **Payee** — who you pay or who pays you. **Category** — which envelope the money will leave. For a paycheck — the month's income. **Account** — which account it's charged to or arrives in. **Date** — the nearest due date. The app counts the next ones from it. **“Repeat”** — how often: twelve options, the sheet is in the second screenshot.   **“Once”** — a payment without repeats. Once it's entered or skipped, it disappears from the list. **“Twice a month”** — on the due day and 15 days after it: the 3rd and the 18th. If the second day doesn't exist in a month, the due date falls on the month's last day. **“Every 4 weeks”** — not the same as “Monthly”: there are 13 due dates a year, not 12, and the date shifts each time. **“Monthly”** and less often — on the same day of the month. If that day doesn't exist in a month, the due date falls on the last day of the month and comes back the next one: a payment on the 31st arrives on February 28, March 31, April 30. **Tags** — the same labels as on transactions. In the screenshot, rent has the “apartment” tag. **“Additional”** — e-receipt, photos and PDFs, “Cleared” and the flag. In the screenshot, a PDF of the lease is attached to the rent.  Everything you fill in here, along with the tags, goes into every transaction entered from this payment. Tags make sense here: every rent payment lands under the “apartment” tag by itself. An attachment, though, is usually needed once: it's enough to attach the lease to one transaction — when you enter the first payment, tap “Edit” and add the PDF in the form. Attached here, it would sit as an icon next to every payment for years to come. Fill in the receipt, photos and PDFs here only if every transaction really needs the document. **“Save”** — the payment appears in the list. If reminders are on, the app will remind you about it.  How to create a payment  “Settings” → “Planning” → “Scheduled payments”. Tap “+ Payment” at the bottom right. “New scheduled payment” opens. Type the amount and tap “Done”. Choose the payee, category and account. “Date” — the nearest due date. “Repeat” — how often it repeats. Optionally — tags and “Additional”. “Save”.  A scheduled transfer A credit card payment, a loan installment, topping up a savings account — that's a transfer between your own accounts. In the “Payee” field, choose an account in the “Transfers” section, and the direction — “Outgoing” or “Incoming”, as with a regular transfer.   The payment shows on **both** accounts' screens, in the “What’s ahead” block: as a minus on checking, as a plus on the loan. On the confirmation screen, in the reminder and in the weekly summary it's named by its route: “Checking → Loan”. “Confirm” records the transfer on both accounts at once, as the form does. Accounts in different currencies — “Credited” and “Rate” appear under the payee: enter the rate right away, when creating it. When the due date comes, “Confirm” opens the form with these numbers — check the day's rate and save. A transfer to an off-budget account (a loan, a deposit) takes money out of an envelope — the app asks for a category, as with a regular transfer. A transfer between budget accounts (checking → credit card) doesn't need a category. In the “Calendar” on “Overview”, a credit card payment isn't shaded as spending: the money stayed in the budget. A payment on an off-budget loan is shaded.  What a scheduled payment can't have A split amount: when you save, the app says “Scheduled splits are not supported yet”. From an existing transaction The fastest way to create a scheduled payment is from a transaction you've already recorded: the form gets everything except the frequency.    “Create a scheduled payment”  Tap a transaction in “Activity”, on an account or category screen — the transaction sheet opens. At the bottom — “Create a scheduled payment”. “New scheduled payment” opens with the same amount, payee, category, account, note, flag and tags. The e-receipt, photos and PDFs, and “Cleared” are empty: each payment has its own. Need to attach, say, a contract? Add it here. The “Repeat” sheet opens on top right away — choose the frequency. The date fills in by itself — the nearest due date after that transaction, but not earlier than today: from a transaction on the 5th, a monthly payment starts on the 5th of next month. “Save”. Only a regular transaction has the button: a split amount and a transfer don't. When it's due On the due date the payment starts waiting for confirmation. It isn't entered by itself: rent might have been paid a day late, and utilities come with a different amount every month. You decide.      Payment card Who, how much, category, account and frequency. The oldest due date at the top.  Entry date It starts as the due date. “‹ ›” move it a day earlier or later, and tapping the date opens a calendar — a month either way. Once moved, “shifted” and “reset” appear next to it (second screenshot); “reset” brings back the due date.  “Confirm” The transaction is recorded on the chosen date and appears in “Activity” with everything the payment holds: tags, receipt, photos and PDFs, the “Cleared” mark. The card goes away, and the due date moves on to the next one.  The next due date is counted from the DUE date, not the entry date: rent due on the 1st was paid on the 3rd — the next due date is still the 1st. Otherwise the schedule would creep with every delay.  “Edit” If the amount is different this time. The transaction form opens with the payment's fields — and with its tags, receipt, photos and PDFs: adjust and save — the transaction is recorded, and the due date is closed. Closed the form without saving? Nothing changed.  “Skip” There was no payment this time. No transaction is recorded, and the due date moves on to the next one. A “Once” payment disappears after a skip.  Didn't open the app for two months? A monthly payment has two due dates behind it. The card shows the oldest; confirm or skip it — the next one appears, until you reach today. When there's nothing left to sort out, the screen says “No payments to confirm”. A scheduled transfer is entered as a transfer — on both accounts at once. If the accounts are in different currencies, “Confirm” opens the form with the “Credited” and “Rate” fields filled in when you created it — adjust to the day's rate and save. Earlier or later than due Money rarely arrives on the exact day. A payment is entered with the date it really happened — and the due date is closed: on its day it won't come up again, neither on the confirmation screen nor as a reminder.  The paycheck came 2 days early The due date hasn't come yet, so it isn't on the confirmation screen.  “Settings” → “Planning” → “Scheduled payments”. Swipe the “Employer” row left — “Enter” appears. Tap it. The transaction form opens: amount, payee, category, account, tags — from the payment, date — today. Money didn't arrive today? Tap the “Date” field and pick the day. “Save”. The paycheck is recorded on the day it arrived. The due date is closed: on its day the app won't remind you or ask you to confirm. The next due date follows the schedule: twice a month — the next of the two days, monthly — a month after the due date, not after the day you recorded it.  Rent was paid a day late The due date has already passed — the payment is waiting on the confirmation screen.  Tap the “Scheduled payments: … awaiting confirmation” banner on “Overview”. In the payment card, tap “›” — the entry date moves a day later. Tap the date itself to open a calendar. “Confirm”. The transaction is recorded on the day you paid. The next due date stays on schedule — the 1st, not the 2nd.  The amount is different this time Utilities are different every month. The due date has come — “Edit” in the card on the confirmation screen; not yet — “Enter” in the list. Correct the amount in the form and tap “Save”: the transaction is recorded with the new amount, and the scheduled payment keeps the old one. What you can do with a row There are no buttons in the row. You swipe the row sideways with your finger — to a button that appears from underneath.      Reminders The app reminds you of a due date with a notification: “Today: …”, “Tomorrow: …” or “In 3 days: …”. When to remind you — on the day of the payment, a day, 2 or 3 days ahead, or a week ahead — at what time, and whether to hide amounts on the lock screen is in [“Settings” → “Reminders”](settings.md#reminders). Where else scheduled payments show up  **“Overview”** — the “What’s ahead” block: upcoming payments with dates, and the “Calendar” in “Scheduled” mode: upcoming due dates, entered ones and ones not entered. More in the article [“Overview”](overview.md#heatmap).  **Account screen** — above the feed, a “What’s ahead” card: this account's scheduled payments. Tapping a row opens “Scheduled payments”.  **“Goals”** — if a category has a scheduled payment, the goal card suggests “From the scheduled payment: …”. More in the article [“Goals”](goals.md#new).  **Weekly summary** — if it's on, it includes upcoming scheduled payments. More in [“Settings” → “Reminders”](settings.md#reminders).
sync: Cloud and backups How not to lose your budget, and how to keep it on several devices. Why all this The budget lives on your phone. This section of the settings answers three questions.   **“My phone fell in the lake”** — three years of budget shouldn't sink along with it. [Backups](#backups) and the cloud help: a new phone [loads the budget from the cloud](#restore).  **“We keep the budget together”** — or it's just you, but with a phone and a computer. All devices look at one cloud and exchange edits: that's [sync](#sync).  **“I messed everything up yesterday”** — deleted the wrong account, imported the wrong file. The app makes [backups on a schedule](#backups) by itself, and you can go back to them.  **Where to start.** Three steps are enough:  [Connect a cloud](#auth) — Google Drive, Dropbox or WebDAV (Nextcloud, ownCloud, pCloud, your own server). [Set a password](#password) if you don't want anyone else to be able to read your data in the cloud. Write it down. That's it. Sync and backups run by themselves from then on: every time you open the app. Authorization: connect a cloud This is where you sign in to a cloud. There are three, and you can connect one or several. In the screenshot Dropbox is already connected, while Google Drive and WebDAV aren't yet: that way you see both kinds of block.    **Cloud encryption** — the same block as on the “Sync” and “Backups” screens. The password is set once — explained [below](#password).  **Google Drive** — “Sign in with Google” — and choose an account. The budget goes into a “My budget” folder on your Google Drive.  After signing in, an account plate replaces the button: name, email, time of the last sync, and “Sign out”. On Google Drive the app sees only what it created itself: other files aren't available to it.  **Dropbox** — “Sign in with Dropbox” opens the Dropbox sign-in page in your browser. You can sign in there in two ways: with your Dropbox email and password, or with the “Continue with Google” button. Allow access — and the browser brings you back to the app. The budget goes into a “My budget” folder.  Signing in with Google ties Dropbox to the Google account you used. A second device, or a second person with a different Google account, can easily end up in a different Dropbox that doesn't have your budget. A Dropbox email and password work the same on any phone or computer, for anyone you keep the budget with.  The main sign-in — coming back from the browser — is usually enough. If the browser never brings you back to the app, expand “Trouble signing in?” → “Sign in with a code (if you were not returned to the app)”: Dropbox shows a code, paste it into the app's dialog. The screenshot shows a connected Dropbox: an account plate with “Sign out” and “Sync now”. “Refresh the Dropbox token” there is a fallback too: only for when sign-in suddenly stops working.  **WebDAV** — your own server or a cloud that speaks WebDAV: Nextcloud, ownCloud, pCloud, Yandex Disk and others. You need an address, a username and a password — no need to sign in to a personal account.  If the cloud has two-factor protection turned on, the server won't accept your regular password: create an “app password” in the cloud's settings and enter that. Start the address with `https://` — with `http://` the username and password travel as plain text, and the app warns you about it.  **The main rule: one cloud account for all devices** The phone, tablet and computer that keep one budget sign in to the cloud with **the same** account. Otherwise each device writes to its own cloud, and they won't see each other's edits.  Create a **separate, new Google account** for the budget and sign in to the app's cloud only with it, on all devices. Don't sign in to your personal account on your wife's phone, or to hers on yours: the phone will start syncing contacts, messages and photos with that account, and two people's personal data will get mixed up. A separate budget account knows only about the budget. **Dropbox** — sign in with your Dropbox **username and password**, not with the “Continue with Google” button. Signing in with Google ties Dropbox to the Google account you used — and on a device with a different Google account it's easy to end up in a different Dropbox that doesn't have your budget. **WebDAV** — the same address, username and password on all devices. Sync Exchanging edits between this device and the cloud, and through the cloud — with your other devices. Add a purchase on the phone — a minute later it's on the computer.    **Cloud encryption** — a password on everything that goes to the cloud. Explained [below](#password).  **Status** — how the last sync ended: “Synced (Dropbox)” in green, an error in red, with a “Report a problem” button.  **Cloud** — if several clouds are connected, choose which one to sync with. No cloud — this spot says “No clouds are connected” and tells you where to connect one.  All devices sync through ONE cloud. The app also refreshes the other connected clouds every few days — in case the main one becomes unavailable.  **Sync photos** — receipt photos and PDFs go to the cloud, into the budget's folder, and appear on other devices. **Right after installing:** off.  Without this switch, transactions arrive on the second device with a photo mark, but the picture itself isn't there. Every photo takes space in the cloud; if you only look at receipts on the phone where you took them, there's no need to turn it on. With a password set, photos are uploaded encrypted.  **Automatic cloud backup from this device** — every automatic backup of the budget also goes to the cloud. **Right after installing:** on.  If two devices keep the budget, both make cloud backups — and you get duplicates. Keep the switch on on one device and turn it off on the others. For the cloud backup to have all receipt photos, also turn on “Sync photos”: otherwise only photos taken on this device go into the backup.  **Sync now** — sync right now. Usually you don't need to tap it — the app does it by itself, see below. When the app syncs by itself  **Every time you open it** — a few seconds after you return to the app. That's why you almost never need to start a sync by hand.  **Not when you minimize it** — Android doesn't let an app keep working after you've minimized it. Edits made before minimizing go up the next time you open it. Want to send them right away? Tap the sync icon on “Overview”.  **The icon on “Overview”** — at the top right. The number on it is how many edits haven't been sent to the cloud yet. Tapping it syncs now.  After each sync, the icon lights up for 15 seconds: green (it worked) or red (it didn't). A single failure is usually the network: the subway, a cabin in the woods. If four syncs in a row fail, the icon stays red until the next one succeeds — that means something broke, and it's worth opening this screen. Press and hold the icon to see the error text. The app stays quiet about automatic syncs. The “Synced” message appears only if you started the sync yourself. If something goes wrong A card appears on the “Sync” screen: what happened and what to do. Here are the kinds.  **“The budget “…” already exists in the cloud with data”** — with the “From cloud” and “Merge” buttons under the card. **What happened.** You connected a cloud, and it already holds a budget with **the same name** as the budget on this device — and both already have data. Usually this is a second phone: someone added accounts or a couple of purchases on it first, and only then connected the first phone's cloud. The app can't tell whether it's one budget or two different ones with the same name, so it touches nothing and waits for your answer. It asks once — on this budget's first sync. **What to choose:**  **This is a second device for the same budget** — tap **“From cloud”**, then “Load”. This device gets the whole budget from the cloud, and what you entered here is lost — enter it again. This is the answer you need most often. **You really did keep one budget on two devices separately** and want to bring it all together — tap **“Merge”**. Everything adds up: what you entered here and what's in the cloud. But accounts and categories you created on each device separately end up side by side — two “Checking” accounts, two “The Corner Cafe” payees — and you'll have to clean up the extras by hand. **These are two different budgets** that just have the same name — for example, yours and your wife's, both “Main budget”. Don't tap either button. Rename the budget on this device: tap the budget name in the “Overview” header → the “⋮” next to this budget → “Rename”. With the new name it gets its own folder in the cloud and syncs separately. Not sure? Make a backup first: “Backups” → “Create a backup now” → “Device”. If the choice turns out to be wrong, you can go back to it.  **“The cloud is password-protected”** — the data in the cloud is encrypted with a password set on another device, and here it isn't set or is different. The data is intact. “Enter password” — enter the same password, and sync continues.  “Password lost” is a last resort: the file in the cloud is replaced with this device's data, and the encryption is removed. Other devices' data isn't lost — their edits come back on their next sync. Before replacing, the app makes backups, and saves the old encrypted file next to them — in case you remember the password.  **“The cloud is not encrypted”** — a password is set on this device, but the data in the cloud is open: encryption was removed on another device. You decide: “Encrypt the cloud” — then the other devices will need to enter the same password — or “Remove the password here”.  **“The sync file in the cloud is unreadable”** — the file in the cloud is damaged and won't fix itself. “Repair the cloud” makes fresh backups of the budget and overwrites the cloud file with this device's data.  Edits from another device that hadn't reached this one yet remain only in the damaged file — a copy of it is saved next to the backups. If the second device works, it brings its data back on its next sync.  **“Photos from the cloud were not decrypted: N”** — the data arrived, but the photos didn't: they're encrypted with a password that isn't set here or is different. Set the same password as on the other device — the photos arrive on the next sync.  **“Conflict”** — the same record was changed on two devices. The card shows how the versions differ: “Keep” keeps this device's version, “Take” takes the cloud's. Cloud encryption: the password The “Cloud encryption” block comes first on the “Authorization”, “Sync” and “Backups” screens. It's one and the same password.  **What it locks** — everything that goes to the cloud: backups, receipt photos and the sync file. The encryption is AES-256. Without a password, anyone with access to the cloud folder can read these files.  **How to set it** — tap “Set a password”.   The “Encryption password” dialog opens. Enter the password in “Password” and again in “Repeat the password” — at least 4 characters. Check “I have written the password down somewhere safe” — without it, “Save” can't be tapped. “Save”. The block becomes “The cloud is password-protected”.  **On other devices** — set **the same** password. The password doesn't sync and goes neither to the cloud nor to the developer — it lives only on the device. With different passwords, sync stops with the “The cloud is password-protected” card.  **Forget the password, and nobody can recover the cloud backups.** Not you, not the developer, not by any means. Write it down where you keep your other important passwords.  **Change or remove it** — in the block, tap “Edit” — “Change the password” or “Turn off encryption”. Change the password on all devices: if one keeps the old one, it stops being able to read the cloud.  **Backups on the phone aren't encrypted** — they sit next to the budget's database itself, and that's open. So when a password is set, “Device” backups in the list carry a “Not encrypted” label — so you don't think everything is locked. Backups A backup is the whole budget at some moment: accounts, categories, transactions, goals, scheduled payments and photos. The app makes backups by itself; you come here when you need to go back.    **Create a backup now** — a backup right now, for example before an import or a big cleanup. The app asks “Where to save the backup?” — screenshot [below](#where).  **“Last backup”** — when the most recent backup of this budget was made. If it's been a while, the line turns yellow.  **Cloud encryption** — the same password as on “Sync” — [above](#password).  **Backup schedule** — how often the app makes backups and how many it keeps. Tap to expand — [below](#schedule).  **Filters** — “All”, “Device” and a chip for each connected cloud. The number is how many backups are there. No clouds connected — no filters: there's nothing to filter.  **Backup** — date and time, where it is, what kind it is and whose budget.  Under the date — where it is (“Device”, “Dropbox”…) and its kind: “Auto, frequent”, “Auto, rare” or “Manual”. Below — the budget name, how many records, photos and PDFs are in the backup, and the file size. The clock-with-arrow icon — **return the budget to this backup**. The trash can — delete the backup (the app asks again).  **The “⋮” menu** — “Restore from a file”, “Readable copy”, “Hints” — [below](#menu). How to return the budget to a backup   Find the backup from the day you need. Not sure which? Take the last one before things went wrong. Tap the clock-with-arrow icon in its row. The “Restore the data?” dialog: “The data will be restored from … The current data will be replaced.” — tap “Restore”. “Restored from …” appears at the bottom. The budget is now as it was at the moment of the backup.  **If a cloud is connected, one restore isn't enough.** A backup is restored to get rid of recent edits: deleted the wrong account, imported the wrong file. But a restore changes the budget only on this phone. The cloud still holds the budget with those very edits, and when syncing, the app combines the phone and the cloud, and the more recent edit wins. Tap “Sync now” — and everything you were getting rid of comes back from the cloud within half a minute. For the rollback to stick, the cloud has to be replaced with the restored budget. How — below. Roll back the cloud too The budget is on one phone — these steps are enough. The order matters.   **Restore the backup** — the steps above. After that, **don't tap “Sync now”**. **Leave the app** with the Home button. While the app is minimized, it doesn't sync. **Delete the sync file in the cloud.** Open the cloud in a browser: the “My budget” folder → the folder named after the budget → the `ynab_budget_sync.json` file. Delete only that — leave the backup and photo folders alone. In Dropbox, the “My budget” folder is inside “Apps” → “My Budget Envelopes”. **Go back to the app.** A few seconds later it syncs by itself, finds no file in the cloud, and puts the restored budget there. The “Sync” screen should say “Synced”.  Every time you return to the app, it syncs a few seconds later. Delete the file first, and when you come back from the browser, the app immediately puts the current budget — still with those edits — into the cloud. Then you'd have to start all over. If several devices keep the budget The second phone and the computer have those edits too. On their sync they'd put them back into the cloud, and from there — back to you. So every other device has to forget its data and take the budget from the cloud afresh — before it gets a chance to sync.   Roll back the budget and the cloud on one device — the steps above. On the other phone, **turn on airplane mode** and only then open the app: without a network it doesn't sync. “Settings” → “About” → “Reset all data”. **Turn off airplane mode.** The app syncs and loads the already rolled-back budget from the cloud. On a computer — the same: disconnect from the internet before launching the program, reset the data in settings, reconnect. Edits on these devices that hadn't reached the cloud yet are lost with the reset. Backup schedule The app makes a backup by itself when it's due — when you open the app and when you switch to another budget. Each budget has its own schedule. There are two kinds of backup: frequent — to go back a few days, and rare — to go back months.    **Default** — frequent backups every 5 days, the last 7 are kept — that's about 35 days back; rare — once a month, 12 are kept — up to a year back.  **Custom** — frequent — every day or every 2, 3, 5, 7 days, keep 3, 5, 7, 10, 14 or 30; rare — once a month or once a quarter, keep 3, 4, 6, 12 or 24 — or “Don't make”.  **“How far back”** — the app works out how many days and months back you can go with the chosen schedule.  **Warnings** — if frequent backups run out before a rare one begins, the app shows “There may be no copies between … and … days” with buttons that close the gap. Choose “Don't make” for rare ones, and it warns that there won't be backups older than a few days.  **Old backups get deleted** — if you reduce how many to keep, the extra backups are deleted at the next automatic backup — both on the phone and in the cloud. So “Save” asks first: how many will be deleted, and the date of the oldest.  **Manual backups** — kept without limit: the schedule doesn't touch them. The schedule applies to this device and doesn't sync.  **The automatic backup failed twice in a row** — a warning “Automatic backup fails” appears on “Overview” with the reason (for example, not enough space) and a “Back up now” button. “Where to save the backup?” “Create a backup now” asks this.    **Device** — to the app's backup folder. The backup appears in the list.  **File on the phone** — choose a folder — for example “Downloads” — and save the backup as a file. You can send it to yourself or put it on a computer. With a password set, the file is encrypted.  **Google Drive, Dropbox, WebDAV** — the backup goes straight to the cloud. Cloud not connected? The app tells you where to connect it. The “⋮” menu     Restore from a file return the budget from a backup file that isn't in the list: downloaded from the cloud, sent to yourself, saved to “Downloads”.  A backup (`.y4zip`), a “Readable copy”, and even the `ynab_budget_sync.json` sync file downloaded from the cloud in a browser all work. If the file is encrypted, the app asks for the password. If the backup is from a different budget (not a single shared account), the app asks again: “This looks like a different budget”. A YNAB 4 file doesn't go here — it's moved over by “Import from YNAB” in the settings.  Readable copy your data as a file any program can open, without a password. Keep it where strangers won't look.  Three options:  **Archive with photos and PDFs** — this budget in full; any archiver opens it. **Data only** — this budget as one text file; any text editor opens it. E-receipts are there, photos and PDFs aren't. **A file from the cloud** — remove the password and compression from a sync file or a cloud backup you downloaded from the cloud in a browser. It's a road to your data that bypasses the app: even without the app, the budget stays yours.  Hints this screen's hints as a list.  Help Center This article on the website: it opens in your browser, in the app's language. Load a budget from the cloud A new phone, a reinstall, or a second device. The budget sits in the cloud under its name; this screen finds it and loads it here. The “I already have a budget” option in the first-launch wizard opens the same screen.    **Connect a cloud** — the same as on the first device: the same Google Drive, Dropbox or WebDAV and **the same account**.  **Choose a budget** — the app shows the budgets in the cloud with the date of their last sync. Tap yours and “Load budget”.  No list, or your budget isn't in it? Tap “Enter the name by hand” and type the name exactly as it's called on the first device: the budget name is the address of its folder in the cloud. Upper and lower case don't matter. The name is shown in the “Overview” header on the first device. If this device already has data, the app asks again: “Replace the data with the cloud copy?”: everything that isn't in the cloud is lost.  **Password** — if a password is set on the first device, set the same one here. Without it, sync stops, and receipt photos arrive but won't open. Local transfer: without a cloud Move a budget between your own devices directly — as a file or over Wi-Fi. No internet and no accounts. It's a one-time transfer, not ongoing sync.    **File** — “Export” — the budget's data as a file: send it through a messenger, by email or on a flash drive. On the other device — “Import” and choose that file.  Import **combines** the data from the file with what's already there, and if the same record differs, it takes the file's version. Photos don't go into the file. To move everything including photos — Wi-Fi or a [backup](#backups) (“Archive with photos and PDFs”).  **WiFi (local network)** — both devices on the same Wi-Fi network. One sends the data, the other receives it and, with “Merge”, sends its own edits back. Photos move too.   On the sending device: “Start the server”. A QR code and a 6-digit “Confirmation code” appear. On the receiving one: “Scan the QR” — the code fills in both fields. Or enter the IP address and the code by hand. “Receive the data”. The app asks “How to apply the data?”: “Merge” — like a regular two-way sync: this device's edits also go to the sending one, nothing is lost; “Replace completely” — this budget becomes an exact copy of the sending one, and everything unsynced here is lost. “Replace” is for a new device. On the sending device — “Stop the server”. The transfer is encrypted with the confirmation code, and the code itself never goes over the network.
settings: Settings What each row does and what it's set to right after installing. The sections are ordered by how often you need them: the most frequent at the top. Planning Everything that repeats: regular payments and reminders.   **Scheduled payments** — rent, subscriptions, a paycheck — everything that repeats. On the day, the app offers to enter the payment with one tap, and “What’s ahead” on “Overview” shows the upcoming ones.  **Reminders** — when and about what the app notifies you. A screen of its own — [below](#reminders). The “Reminders” screen    **Scheduled payments** — “When to remind” — on the day of the payment, 1, 2 or 3 days ahead, or a week ahead; “Reminder time”; “Hide amounts in notifications” — the reminder shows on the lock screen, and without this anyone who picks up the phone can read the amount. **Right after installing:** the day before, at 9:00 AM, amounts visible.  **Daily spending** — “Remind me to add spending” — in the evening, if you haven't recorded anything today. If you have, it stays quiet. **Right after installing:** off, at 9:00 PM.  **Weekly summary** — “Send a summary” — on the last day of the week: how much was spent and on what the most, which categories are running out, which scheduled payments are coming. **Right after installing:** off.  **All reminders** — “Reminders at the exact time”. Without permission, Android is allowed to deliver a reminder late. The switch opens the Android settings where that permission is granted. Data The budget's lists and exchanging data with other programs.   **Payees and Tags** — lists that build up by themselves as you record transactions. All about them — in the article [“Payees and tags”](payees-tags.md).  **Export to CSV** — all of the current budget's transactions as a spreadsheet file — to open in Excel or Google Sheets.  The file has everything a transaction has: date, account, payee, category and its group, amount and currency, “cleared”, note, the parts of a split amount, transfer, tags, flag, e-receipts, the budget month (for a paycheck recorded “for next month” — the month it's set aside for), and for a transfer between currencies — how much arrived, in what currency and at what rate. Only photos and PDFs aren't exported: they're files on the phone. Column names are in English (`date`, `amount`, `tags`…) and don't depend on the app's language: that way formulas and pivot tables don't break if you change the language. Numbers in the file are always real, even if “Hide amounts” is on. The field separator follows the number format, so the table opens as columns rather than one line.  **Import from YNAB** — move a budget from YNAB 4 (a .y4backup file) or from web YNAB (a .zip export): accounts, categories and the whole history. After the import, a glossary shows what each YNAB term is called here.  **Inbox** — at the checkout, just the amount; you choose the account and category later. How it works — in the article [“Transaction form”](entry.md). **Right after installing:** off. Sync The cloud, backups and moving a budget between devices. Here briefly what's where; in detail — the article [“Cloud and backups”](sync.md).   **Authorization** — connect a cloud: Google Drive, Dropbox or WebDAV. The main rule: all devices that keep this budget use **the same cloud account**, otherwise they won't see each other.  **If family members have different Google accounts**, create a **separate, new Google account** for the budget and sign in to the app's cloud only with it, on all devices. Don't sign in to your personal account on your wife's phone, or to hers on yours: the phone will start syncing contacts, messages and photos with that account, and two people's personal data will get mixed up. A separate budget account knows only about the budget. **Dropbox** — sign in with your Dropbox **username and password**, not with the “Continue with Google” button. Signing in with Google ties Dropbox to the Google account you used — and on a device with a different Google account it's easy to end up in a different Dropbox that doesn't have your budget. A Dropbox username and password work the same on any device. **WebDAV** — a cloud that supports it (Nextcloud, ownCloud, pCloud and others) or your own server; the same address, username and folder on all devices.  **Sync** — exchanging edits with the cloud and other devices; also the password that encrypts the cloud, and the sync log.  **Backups** — copies of the budget: automatic on a schedule and manual, on the phone and in the cloud. Also from here — a “Readable copy” as a file.  **Load budget from cloud** — a new phone or a reinstall — the budget comes back from the cloud or from a backup file.  **Local transfer** — move a budget between your own devices over WiFi or as a file — without a cloud. Budget Settings for the current budget.   **Budget currency** — the symbol you keep your budget in. Only for this budget; the app doesn't convert amounts — only the symbol changes.  **“Pay yourself” categories** — which categories count as “set aside for yourself” — usually savings. With none selected, there's no “Pay yourself” block on “Overview”. What it shows — in the article [“Overview”](overview.md).  **Age of money** — how to calculate it: three ways. A screen of its own — [below](#aom). The “Age of money” screen   The three ways are described right on the screen. Which is closer to the truth and why, with examples — in the article [“Overview”](overview.md), section “Age of money in detail”. In short: **“Savings-aware”** counts exactly the money that's in your accounts. **Right after installing:** “Classic (YNAB FIFO)”. Security A lock on the app.   **PIN** — the app asks for it when opening. Once a PIN is set, “Biometric unlock” appears below — a fingerprint or face instead of digits.  Without a PIN, biometrics can't be turned on: there's no lock without it. While a PIN is set, the app's card in the list of open apps is covered, and prying eyes won't see your balances there (on Android 13 and newer). Appearance Two screens: language with formats, and the whole look of the app.   **Language and formats** — the interface language, how amounts and dates look, how to type an amount. The screen — [below](#formats).  **Appearance** — theme, style, font, icons and how a transaction row looks. The screen — [below](#appearance). The “Language and formats” screen    **Interface language** — thirteen languages; “System default” is the phone's language. The language lives on this device and doesn't sync: the phone can be in English and the computer in German.  **Amount format** — thousands and decimal separators, which side the currency symbol goes on. By default — as is usual for the chosen language: “$1,234,567.89”.  **Amount entry** — “With a decimal point” or “From cents, like a card terminal” (1-2-5-0 means 12.50). **Right after installing:** with a decimal point.  **Amount keypad** — “For the right hand” — digits on the right, operators on the left; “For the left hand” — the other way round. **Right after installing:** for the right hand.  **Date format** — order, separator, month as a number or a word — 24 options to choose from. The “Appearance” screen    **Theme** — “System”, “Light” or “Dark”. “System” follows the phone.  **Style** — the app's color character: “Classic”, “Neon”, “Aurora”, “Acid”, “Candy”, “Marshmallow”, “Graphite”. Each has a light and a dark version.  **Corners** — “Sharp”, “Standard” or “Soft” — the corners of cards, buttons and chips. Independent of the style.  **Income and spending colours** — “Standard” — income in green, spending in red. “Reinforced” — income in blue: for those who find it hard to tell green from red.  About one man in twelve and one woman in two hundred see colors differently. There are three kinds:  **deuteranopia** — weaker perception of green; the most common; **protanopia** — weaker perception of red; **tritanopia** — blue and yellow get confused; very rare. With the first two, green and red merge into a similar brownish color, and income can't be told from spending by color. Both of these see blue well — that's why in “Reinforced” income is blue. **What else the app does for these people — already, without any setting:**  every amount has a “+” or “−” sign: the direction of a transaction is visible with no color at all (and right after installing, transaction amounts have no color anyway); overspending speaks not only with color but with an icon too: a wallet — you spent your own money, a card — you went into credit card debt; a sync that failed changes not only the icon's color but its drawing too — a “!” appears inside; the colors of report charts are chosen so that neighboring slices differ in brightness too, not just in hue. **What “Reinforced” changes:** income in blue everywhere — in amounts, in the income form's header, in the charts and in the “Income and expenses” table; transaction flag colors are spread apart by brightness; the report charts and “Money flow” use their own color set. Each set is checked against all three kinds during development. “Reinforced” also helps those who tell colors apart well but look at the screen in bright sunlight.  **Font** — the system font or one of seven: “Fira Sans”, “Geologica”, “IBM Plex Sans”, “Inter”, “Manrope”, “Noto Sans”, “Source Sans 3” — for the whole interface.  **Density** — “Compact”, “Standard” or “Comfortable” — the space between rows and blocks. The size of the letters doesn't change.  **Icons** — “Standard” or “Two-tone”.  **Transaction amount colours** — whether to color amounts in transaction lists: “No colour”, “Income only” or “Spending and income”.  **Right after installing — “No colour”**, and every screenshot in this guide was taken that way. Why: red is the color of alarm, and buying bread doesn't deserve an alarm; when every row glows red, the color stops saying anything. The sign shows the direction of a transaction: “−” for spending, “+” for income. Want color? Choose “Spending and income” or “Income only”. Category overspending, debt and sync state stay colored whatever you choose: there, color is a warning.  **Flag shape** — “Dot”, “Triangle flag” or “Wavy flag” — how the flag looks in transaction rows.  **Return to** — “Overview” — after a break of more than 30 seconds and at launch, “Overview” opens; “Where you left off” — the same screen, even with a form open. The PIN is asked in both cases. Help & contact Hints and getting in touch with the developer.   **Hints** — all of the app's hints as a list, by screen. Also “Show hints again”. One screen's hints are also opened by the “Hints” item in its “⋮” menu.  **Help Center** — articles about every screen on the website, in the app's language; this item opens the main page. One screen's article is opened by the “Help Center” item in its “⋮” menu.  **Telegram chat** — a group where questions get answered and where you can ask other users.  **Report a problem** — an email to the developer. The app and device versions are filled in by themselves; you can attach the event log from “About”.  **Suggest an improvement** — an email with an idea: what's awkward now and how you'd like it. About One row, and behind it a screen with the version, documents and service items.   **About** — the screen — [below](#about-screen). The “About” screen    **Version** — the version number; tap it for “What is new”: what changed in the latest releases.  **Windows version** — the same budget on a computer — in the Microsoft Store.  **Share the app** — send a link to the app on Google Play.  **Privacy policy and License** — documents. In short: your data is yours, and the developer has no access to it.  **Event log** — app and sync errors. Useful if you're writing about a problem.  **Reset all data** — delete all accounts, categories, transactions, scheduled payments and goals. The app asks again: “Reset all data?”. This can't be undone.  If sync is connected, the data comes back from the cloud on the next sync. To delete it for good, disconnect the cloud or delete the sync file in it. Before resetting, make a copy in “Backups”.
